name: Alabama A&M University
formerNames: Huntsville State Normal School for Negroes
State Normal and Industrial School of Huntsville
The State Agricultural and Mechanical College for Negroes
State Agricultural and Mechanical Institute for Negroes
description: Founded in 1875 by formerly enslaved educator William Hooper Councill as a normal school in Huntsville, it became Alabama's 1890 land-grant institution. Sitting next to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center and Redstone Arsenal, AAMU feeds Huntsville's aerospace and defense-contracting economy — alumni include Hall of Famer-turned-contractor John Stallworth (Madison Research Corp.) and EyeMail founder Lisa S. Jones.

facts.d: William Hooper Councill, the first president, opened the school in 1875 as Huntsville State Normal School for Negroes.
It became the State Agricultural and Mechanical College for Negroes in 1896 and took its present name in 1969.
Alumni work across Huntsville's NASA and defense-contracting cluster; Stallworth's MRC and Cynthia Crutchfield's career both grew from it.

name: Alabama State University
affiliation: Thurgood Marshall College Fund; American Missionary Association (early support)
description: Begun in 1867 as the Lincoln Normal School in Marion by nine formerly enslaved men, it moved to Montgomery in 1887 under president William Burns Paterson. ASU students, faculty and alumni were central to the Montgomery Bus Boycott — Ralph Abernathy, Fred Gray and Jo Ann Robinson's network — and the school still anchors Montgomery's Black professional class.

facts.d: The Lincoln Normal School of Marion (1867) relocated to Montgomery in 1887 and became Alabama State University in 1969.
Alumni include Ralph Abernathy, attorney Fred Gray and Fred Shuttlesworth; ASU faculty helped print boycott leaflets in 1955.
ASU's Mobile extension center (1927) became today's Bishop State Community College.

connections.label: AMA supported the early Lincoln Normal School

name: Bishop State Community College
formerNames: S. D. Bishop State Junior College
description: Begun in 1927 as the Mobile extension of Alabama State College and made a junior college in 1936, Bishop State absorbed Southwest State Technical College and Carver State Technical College in 1991. It is Mobile's public HBCU for workforce and transfer education.

facts.d: Started as Alabama State's Mobile center; named for first president S. D. Bishop in 1971.
Southwest State Technical (est. 1947) and Carver State Technical (est. 1962) were consolidated into it in 1991.

name: C. A. Fredd State Technical College
fate: Merged into Shelton State Community College in 1994, which now operates the Fredd campus.
description: Created by the Alabama legislature in 1963 as the Tuscaloosa State Trade School for Black students, renamed Tuscaloosa State Technical College in 1974 and C. A. Fredd State Technical College in 1976. Its 1994 merger gave Shelton State its HBCU status.

facts.d: Trade school (1963), Tuscaloosa State Technical College (1974), C. A. Fredd State Technical College (1976).
Became part of Shelton State Community College.

name: Concordia College Alabama
fate: Closed after the spring 2018 semester, citing years of financial distress and declining enrollment.
description: Opened in 1922 in a rented cottage after Black Lutheran congregations in Alabama's Black Belt — built largely through educator Rosa J. Young — petitioned the Missouri Synod. It was the only historically Black member of the Concordia University System and closed in 2018.

facts.d: The sole HBCU in the LCMS's Concordia University System.
Educator Rosa J. Young, who taught there, is credited with building the Black Lutheran congregations behind it.

name: Daniel Payne College
fate: A 1977 tornado badly damaged the campus; with mounting debts it filed for bankruptcy in 1978 and closed in 1979.
description: Founded in Selma in 1889 by the AME Church and named for Bishop Daniel Payne — the first Black college president in the U.S. — it moved to Birmingham in 1922. Airport and interstate expansion forced relocations, and a tornado in 1977 led to its closure.

facts.d: Bishop Daniel Payne was the AME's sixth bishop and led Wilberforce University.
Relocated to Woodlawn in Birmingham in 1922; moved again in 1974.

name: Gadsden State Community College
description: Formed in 1985 by merging several Gadsden-area colleges, it carries HBCU designation through the Gadsden Vocational Trade School, opened in 1960 for Black students and later renamed Gadsden State Technical Institute — today its Valley Street Campus. The school was designated a historically Black college in 1997.

facts.d: The Valley Street Campus descends from the 1960 Gadsden Vocational Trade School for Black students; designated HBCU in 1997.
Combines the Alabama School of Trades (1925), Gadsden State Junior College (1965) and Ayers State Technical College (2003).

name: H. Councill Trenholm State Community College
formerNames: H. Councill Trenholm State Technical College
description: A public historically Black technical and community college in Montgomery named for Alabama State president H. Councill Trenholm. Its 2001 consolidation with John M. Patterson Technical College kept the Trenholm name to preserve Title III-B HBCU funding.

facts.d: The consolidated name kept Title III-B eligibility that the historically Black college held before the merger.
Renamed from State Technical College to Community College.

sources.label: Wikipedia — H. Councill Trenholm State Community College

name: J. F. Drake State Community and Technical College
formerNames: J. F. Drake State Technical College
description: Opened in 1961 in Huntsville as a vocational-technical school for Black students and named for Alabama A&M president Joseph Fanning Drake, Drake State trains technicians for Huntsville's aerospace, manufacturing and defense economy.

facts.d: Honors Joseph Fanning Drake, longtime president of Alabama A&M.
Feeds technicians into the Huntsville aerospace/defense cluster.

sources.label: Wikipedia — J. F. Drake State Technical College
Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Lawson State Community College
formerNames: Theodore Alfred Lawson State Junior College
description: Started in 1949 as Wenonah State Technical Institute; joined with Wenonah State Junior College in 1973 and was named for first president Theodore Alfred Lawson. It absorbed Bessemer State Technical College in 2005.

facts.d: Technical and junior-college divisions merged in 1973 as T. A. Lawson State.
Bessemer State Technical College became its Bessemer Campus in 2005.

name: Miles College
description: Founded in 1898 by the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church just west of Birmingham, Miles was a staging ground for the Birmingham civil-rights movement and the 1962 Selective Buying Campaign — a student-led economic boycott of downtown merchants. Alumni include Birmingham's first Black mayor Richard Arrington Jr., Alabama's first Black federal judge U. W. Clemon, and insurance executive-congressman Bennett M. Stewart.

facts.d: Organized by the CME Church; named Miles Memorial College until 1941.
Miles students launched the 1962 boycott of Birmingham stores that refused to hire Black clerks — an early use of consumer economic power.
Produced Birmingham mayor Richard Arrington Jr. and judge U. W. Clemon.

name: Oakwood University
description: Opened in 1896 by the General Conference of Seventh-day Adventists on a former plantation in Huntsville, Oakwood is the only HBCU owned and operated by the Adventist church. It is known for its music (the Aeolians choir, Take 6) and ministry training; alumni include insurance entrepreneur and civil-rights leader T. R. M. Howard and Senate Chaplain Barry Black.

facts.d: Sponsored by the General Conference until 2014, then by the North American Division.
Touring choir founded in 1946 by Dr. Eva B. Dykes; has performed at the White House and Kennedy Center.
Joined the United Negro College Fund in 1964.

connections.label: founded by the SDA General Conference

name: Selma University
formerNames: Alabama Baptist Normal and Theological School
description: Founded in 1878 by Alabama's Black Baptist convention to train ministers and teachers, it took the Selma University name in 1908. Its graduates include civil-rights leader Fred Shuttlesworth, Juanita Abernathy and federal-workers union president Everett Kelley.

facts.d: The Black Baptist convention voted in 1877 to locate the school in Selma; William H. McAlpine was among the founders.
Became Selma University on May 14, 1908.

connections.label: founded by Alabama's Black Baptist convention

name: Shelton State Community College
description: Tuscaloosa's community college, established under its current name in 1979, gained its historically Black designation through the 1994 merger with C. A. Fredd State Technical College, the city's Black technical college; the Fredd campus continues as part of Shelton State.

facts.d: C. A. Fredd State Technical College merged into Shelton State in 1994.
Formed when Shelton State combined with the Tuscaloosa branch of Brewer State.

name: Stillman College
description: Authorized by the (Southern) Presbyterian General Assembly in 1875 and opened in 1876 on the idea of pastor Charles Allen Stillman to train Black ministers, it became a four-year college in 1948. Alumni include Marine Lt. Gen. Willie J. Williams, legislator Michael Figures and Olympic long-jump champion Jeff Henderson.

facts.d: Conceived 'for the training of colored men for the ministry' by Charles A. Stillman of First Presbyterian, Tuscaloosa.
Tuscaloosa Institute (1876–1895), Stillman Institute (1895–1948), Stillman College (1948–).

name: Talladega College
affiliation: American Missionary Association; United Church of Christ; UNCF
description: Alabama's oldest private historically Black liberal-arts college, begun in 1867 by formerly enslaved men William Savery and Thomas Tarrant with American Missionary Association and Freedmen's Bureau support. Talladega produced a striking roster of business pioneers — ad-agency founder Barbara Gardner Proctor, millionaire dermatologist-banker Theodore K. Lawless, Walker Company manager Willard Ransom and Pepsi bottler William R. Harvey.

facts.d: Savery and Tarrant met at a Freedmen's Bureau convention in Mobile in 1866; the AMA bought the building and the Bureau the land.
Hale Woodruff's murals in Savery Library anchor the William R. Harvey Museum of Art (opened 2020).
Alumni founded or led Proctor & Gardner Advertising, Service Federal Savings and Loan and the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Co.

name: Tuskegee University
formerNames: Tuskegee Normal School for Colored Teachers
description: Chartered in 1881 after an agreement between Black community leader Lewis Adams and former Confederate colonel Wilbur F. Foster, with Booker T. Washington as first principal. Tuskegee became the flagship of Washington's self-help and industrial-education philosophy, home to George Washington Carver's research and the training ground of the Tuskegee Airmen. Its economic legacy runs from Washington's National Negro Business League to alumni such as builder Herman J. Russell, broadcaster Tom Joyner and inventor-entrepreneur Lonnie Johnson.

facts.d: Lewis Adams secured state funding for a Black normal school in exchange for delivering Black votes to Wilbur F. Foster; Booker T. Washington opened the school on July 4, 1881.
Washington founded the National Negro Business League in 1900; Tuskegee alumni such as Jake Simmons Jr. later presided over it.
Tuskegee trained the Tuskegee Airmen in WWII and today describes itself as a leading producer of Black aerospace engineers (self-reported).

connections.label: Booker T. Washington founded the NNBL, 1900

name: Arkansas Baptist College
kind: Private HBCU · Baptist liberal arts college
affiliation: Consolidated Missionary Baptist State Convention of Arkansas
description: Founded in 1884 as the Minister's Institute and funded by the Colored Baptists of Arkansas, it is the only historically Black Baptist college west of the Mississippi. Its 1893 Main Building is on the National Register. Alumni include 'King of the Jukebox' Louis Jordan.

facts.t: Only Black Baptist college west of the Mississippi.
facts.d: Per Wikipedia.

connections.label: Colored Baptists of the State of Arkansas

name: Arkansas-Haygood Industrial College
location: Washington, AR; later Jefferson County, AR
fate: Relocated to Jefferson County in 1927 and closed during World War II (exact year not documented).
description: Haygood Seminary was one of the first institutions established by the CME Church, training Black Arkansans for the ministry near Washington, Arkansas. It moved in 1927 and operated as Arkansas-Haygood Industrial College until closing during World War II.

facts.d: One of the first institutions founded by the CME Church.

name: Philander Smith University
description: Founded in 1877 as Walden Seminary by the Methodist Episcopal Church and renamed in 1882 for donor Philander Smith, it became Philander Smith University in 2023. A UNCF founding member, it absorbed the assets of Missouri's George R. Smith College. Alumni include Surgeon General Joycelyn Elders, theologian James Cone and Stax Records co-owner Al Bell.

facts.d: Al Bell, listed among alumni, became co-owner of Stax Records in 1969 and later president of Motown Records.
Renamed Philander Smith University on August 1, 2023.

name: Shorter College
description: Founded in 1886 as Bethel University by the AME Church's Twelfth Episcopal District, it became Shorter College in 1903. One of the few private Black junior colleges, its alumni include Daisy Bates, publisher of the Arkansas State Press and mentor of the Little Rock Nine, and lawyer Scipio Africanus Jones.

facts.d: Civil rights leader and newspaper publisher Daisy Bates is listed among alumni.

name: Southland College
fate: The Quakers' Home Mission Board 'laid down' the school at the end of the 1925 school year for lack of funds.
description: Begun in 1864 by Indiana Quakers Alida and Calvin Clark as an orphanage for Black children in Union-occupied Helena, Southland became the first institution of higher education for African Americans west of the Mississippi River.

facts.d: Recognized as the first Black higher-education institution west of the Mississippi.

name: University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff
formerNames: Arkansas Agricultural, Mechanical and Normal College (Arkansas AM&N)
description: Authorized in 1873 and opened in 1875 as Branch Normal College, it became Arkansas AM&N in 1927 and UAPB in 1972. Martin Luther King Jr. gave its 1958 commencement address. Alumni include Congressman Danny K. Davis, transplant pioneer Samuel L. Kountz and Steelers great L. C. Greenwood; it is known today for aquaculture.

facts.d: Rejoined the University of Arkansas System in 1972 as UAPB.
Samuel L. Kountz (1952) performed the first successful kidney transplant between non-identical humans.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff

name: District of Columbia Teachers College
fate: Consolidated with Federal City College and Washington Technical Institute into the University of the District of Columbia in 1977.
description: Formed on July 1, 1955 by merging the historically Black Miner Teachers College with the white Wilson Teachers College in response to Brown v. Board, D.C. Teachers College carried Miner's mission of training the city's public-school teachers. Graduates include federal Chief Judge Norma Holloway Johnson and D.C. schools superintendent Floretta Dukes McKenzie.

facts.d: Created in 1955 from Miner (Black) and Wilson (white) teachers colleges following Brown v. Board of Education.
Supplied much of the D.C. public-school teaching corps until its 1977 consolidation into UDC.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of the District of Columbia (history)

name: Federal City College
kind: Public HBCU predecessor · Liberal arts college
affiliation: Public; land-grant under the 1966 D.C. School Reform Act
fate: Consolidated into the University of the District of Columbia on August 1, 1977.
description: Created by Congress in the 1966 District of Columbia School Reform Act and opened in 1968, Federal City College was planned as a small, selective liberal-arts college but drew 6,000 applications in its first year and admitted about 1,400 students by lottery. Its predominantly Black, open-access student body made it a launchpad for D.C. journalists, activists and officials, including broadcaster Kojo Nnamdi.

facts.d: When it opened in 1968, applications soared to 6,000 and some 1,400 students were placed by lottery.
Both it and Washington Technical Institute received land-grant status and a $7.24 million endowment in lieu of land.
It was accredited in 1974, three years before the UDC consolidation.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of the District of Columbia (history)

name: Frelinghuysen University
kind: Private HBCU · Adult and evening university
affiliation: Independent; founded by Jesse and Rosetta Lawson
formerNames: Frelinghuysen Group of Schools for Colored Working People
fate: Lost accreditation in 1937 after Depression-era financial trouble, stopped awarding degrees, and had closed by 1964.
description: Founded in 1906 by activists Jesse and Rosetta Lawson, Frelinghuysen was the first school to offer evening and extension courses to Black working adults in Washington, holding classes in homes and businesses to cut commuting time and charging the lowest tuition possible. Scholar Anna J. Cooper served as president from 1930. It was accredited and awarded degrees from 1927 to 1937, and its John M. Langston School of Law fed faculty to the later Terrell Law School.

facts.d: Classes ran in local homes and businesses, with programs from basic literacy through undergraduate and graduate courses.
The renowned educator and author succeeded Jesse Lawson as president, taking office in 1930.
Frelinghuysen was accredited and awarded degrees from 1927 until 1937.

name: Howard University
kind: Private HBCU · Federally chartered research university
affiliation: Federally chartered (Congress, 1867); founded by members of the First Congregational Society of Washington; named for Freedmen's Bureau commissioner Gen. Oliver O. Howard
description: Chartered by Congress on March 2, 1867, Howard grew from a proposed seminary for Black clergy into a comprehensive university with liberal arts, medicine, law, business, communications and engineering. It is the only HBCU with an R1 research classification and receives an annual congressional appropriation. Its law school trained the NAACP legal team that won Brown v. Board, and its alumni network is the largest in this map — spanning Wall Street, broadcasting, hospitality, construction and the presidency's line of succession.

facts.t: Named for a Freedmen's Bureau chief.
facts.d: Gen. Oliver Otis Howard, commissioner of the Freedmen's Bureau, was a founder and served as university president from 1869 to 1874.
Howard is the only historically Black university classified as an R1 (very high research activity) doctoral university.
A 2018 Bloomberg Businessweek survey found 25 of 49 Howard School of Business graduates from 2010–2012 had started a company — the highest founder share among surveyed business schools.
Its radio station WHUR launched Cathy Hughes's broadcasting career; in 2016 the School of Communications was renamed for her after a multimillion-dollar gift from Alfred C. Liggins III.

sources.label: Bloomberg Businessweek — Best B-Schools 2018: alumni startups

connections.label: founded by Freedmen's Bureau commissioner O. O. Howard
founded by members of the First Congregational Society of Washington (Congregationalist)

name: Miner Teachers College
affiliation: Founded by abolitionist Myrtilla Miner with Quaker support; later part of the D.C. public school system
fate: In 1955, after Brown v. Board, it merged with the white Wilson Teachers College to form District of Columbia Teachers College.
description: Myrtilla Miner, a white abolitionist teacher from New York, opened the Normal School for Colored Girls in 1851 against mob hostility and official opposition, funded by Quakers and a $1,000 gift from Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin royalties. Reopened after the Civil War as Miner Normal School, it joined the D.C. public schools in 1879 and became the four-year Miner Teachers College in 1929, training generations of Black D.C. teachers. Its 1913 Georgia Avenue building is on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.t: Fourth normal school in the U.S.
facts.d: It was the first normal school in D.C. and the fourth in the nation; enrollment grew from 6 to 40 within two months.
Benefactors included Quakers, Henry Ward Beecher and Harriet Beecher Stowe; Johns Hopkins sat on its 1856 board of trustees.
Congress made Miner Normal School a four-year teachers college in 1929.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Normal School for Colored Girls / Miner Teachers College

name: Robert H. Terrell Law School
affiliation: Independent; founded by George A. Parker and other Black D.C. lawyers
fate: Closed in 1950 after graduating about 600 lawyers, as other D.C. law schools integrated.
description: Founded in 1931 after Howard University ended its evening law program, Terrell Law School let working Black Washingtonians study law at night and, over 19 years, educated the majority of Black law students in the city. It was named for Robert Heberton Terrell, the long-serving Black judge of the D.C. Municipal Court. Alumni include D.C. Court of Appeals judge Austin L. Fickling, civil-rights leader Ruby Hurley and D.C. Council member Wilhelmina Rolark.

facts.d: Its founders created it when Howard closed its evening law school program.
The school graduated roughly 600 lawyers before closing in 1950.

connections.label: founding dean George A. Parker came from Frelinghuysen's Langston School of Law

name: University of the District of Columbia
affiliation: Public (District of Columbia); land-grant status under the 1966 D.C. School Reform Act; Thurgood Marshall College Fund member
formerNames: Normal School for Colored Girls (earliest predecessor)
Miner Normal School / Miner Teachers College (predecessor)
description: UDC is the only public university in Washington, D.C. It was formed on August 1, 1977, by consolidating Federal City College, Washington Technical Institute and District of Columbia Teachers College, and traces its founding to Myrtilla Miner's 1851 Normal School for Colored Girls. A commuter-heavy urban land-grant, it added the David A. Clarke School of Law in 1996 and a community college in 2009, and has long served working adults — including future media CEO Alfred C. Liggins III, who took night classes there.

facts.d: Its earliest predecessor, Myrtilla Miner's Normal School for Colored Girls, opened December 3, 1851 with six students — the first normal school in D.C.
Federal City College, Washington Technical Institute and D.C. Teachers College were consolidated on August 1, 1977, with Lisle C. Carter as first president.
The 1966 D.C. School Reform Act gave its predecessors land-grant status with a $7.24 million endowment in lieu of land.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of the District of Columbia

name: Washington Technical Institute
affiliation: Public; land-grant under the 1966 D.C. School Reform Act
fate: Consolidated into the University of the District of Columbia on August 1, 1977.
description: Established under the 1966 D.C. School Reform Act as the city's public technical school, Washington Technical Institute opened its Van Ness campus in 1968 in buildings vacated by the National Bureau of Standards — today UDC's flagship campus. It was accredited in 1971 and trained D.C. residents in applied technical and vocational fields.

facts.d: WTI's 1968 campus on the former National Bureau of Standards site became UDC's main campus.
It earned accreditation in 1971 before merging into UDC in 1977.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of the District of Columbia (history and campus)

name: Wayland Seminary
kind: Private HBCU · Baptist seminary and college
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society (National Theological Institute)
fate: In 1899 it merged with Richmond Theological Seminary to form Virginia Union University in Richmond.
description: Wayland Seminary began in 1867 in the basement of Washington's First Colored Baptist Church (later Nineteenth Street Baptist) as the D.C. branch of the American Baptist Home Mission Society's National Theological Institute, named for anti-slavery Brown University president Francis Wayland. Led for 30 years by abolitionist George M. P. King, it offered ministerial, college, high-school and preparatory courses to freedmen and women. Its alumni include Booker T. Washington and Abyssinian Baptist pastor Adam Clayton Powell Sr.

facts.d: Wikipedia's alumni list for Wayland includes Booker T. Washington and Adam Clayton Powell Sr.
A new Wayland building opened in 1875 on land in today's Meridian Hill Park; it was demolished around 1900.
ABHMS combined Wayland with Richmond Theological Seminary in 1899 to create Virginia Union University.

name: Delaware State University
description: Created by the Delaware General Assembly on May 15, 1891, under the Second Morrill Act as the Delaware College for Colored Students, it was renamed in 1893 to avoid confusion with the white Delaware College in Newark. It lost accreditation in 1949, regained it in 1957, and became a university in 1993. In 2021 it acquired Methodist-founded Wesley College — the first HBCU to acquire a non-HBCU institution.

facts.d: Established by the state legislature in 1891 to give Delaware a Black land-grant college.
Provisionally accredited in 1945, revoked in 1949, restored in 1957.
In 2021 DSU absorbed Wesley College, now 'DSU Downtown' — a first for an HBCU.
Auto dealer Steve Ewing ('83) gave $1 million in 2023, the largest single gift by an alumnus in school history.

sources.label: Atlanta Tribune — Steve Ewing donates $1 million to alma mater

name: Bethune-Cookman University
formerNames: Daytona Educational and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls
Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute for Girls
description: Founded in 1904 by Mary McLeod Bethune as a school for Black girls in a rented house in Daytona; it merged with Jacksonville's Cookman Institute for boys (1872) in 1923. Bethune was also an insurance founder and investor, and the school's alumni include Harry T. Moore and Madam C. J. Walker executive Marjorie Joyner.

facts.d: Bethune opened the school in 1904 with six students and 50-cent tuition.
Joined with Cookman Institute in 1923 (name Daytona Cookman Collegiate Institute by 1927); Bethune-Cookman College from 1941, university from 2007.

name: Booker T. Washington Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Nominally merged with Pensacola Junior College in 1965.
description: The first of Florida's twelve public Black junior colleges, opened in Pensacola in 1949. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1949–1965.

name: Carver Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1963, among the first of the Black junior colleges to shut as Florida desegregated.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education to sustain "separate but equal." Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1960–1963.

name: Collier-Blocker Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1964 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1960–1964.

name: Cookman Institute
fate: Merged with Mary McLeod Bethune's Daytona school in 1923 to form what became Bethune-Cookman University.
description: Founded in Jacksonville in 1872 by Rev. D. S. Darnell under Methodist sponsorship, Cookman was one of Florida's first institutions of higher learning for Black students. A. Philip Randolph graduated as valedictorian in 1907; Florida's first Black judge, James Dean, also attended.

facts.d: A. Philip Randolph was valedictorian of Cookman's 1907 class.
Combined with the Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute.

name: Edward Waters University
formerNames: East Florida Scientific and Divinity High School
description: Florida's first independent institution of higher education and first HBCU, founded in 1866 by members of the AME Church in Jacksonville. Renamed for AME bishop Edward Waters in 1892, it became a university in 2021. Negro leagues great Buck O'Neil finished high school and two years of college there.

facts.d: Founded 1866, the year after the Civil War ended.
Centennial Hall (1916) is on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Florida A&M University
affiliation: State University System of Florida; 1890 land-grant
formerNames: State Normal College for Colored Students
State Normal and Industrial College for Colored Students
Florida Agricultural and Mechanical College for Negroes
description: Founded October 3, 1887, as the State Normal College for Colored Students. FAMU's School of Business and Industry, built by founding dean Sybil Collins Mobley, is a major pipeline of corporate executives, among them Microsoft chairman John W. Thompson, Helen of Troy CEO Scott Uzzell, Independence Blue Cross CEO Gregory Deavens and Northern Trust leaders Shundrawn Thomas and Lyle Logan.

facts.d: Founding dean Sybil Mobley sat on the boards of Anheuser-Busch, Sears, Hershey and others and built an executive-style business school.
SBI's Big Board, begun in 1983, honors donors of at least $100,000 each in endowed scholarships.
Florida A&M College for Negroes became Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University in 1953.

name: Florida Memorial University
formerNames: Florida Normal and Industrial Memorial College
description: Traces to the Florida Baptist Institute (Live Oak, 1879) and the Florida Baptist Academy (Jacksonville, later St. Augustine), which combined and moved to Miami Gardens. James Weldon and J. Rosamond Johnson wrote "Lift Ev'ry Voice and Sing" there in 1900. Alumni include aviator Barrington Irving and civil rights martyr Harry T. Moore.

facts.d: "Lift Ev'ry Voice and Sing" was written in 1900 by the Johnson brothers; Rosamond taught at the school.
The Live Oak and St. Augustine institutions merged in 1941; university status in 2006.

name: Gibbs Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Placed under St. Petersburg Junior College midway through 1964–65 and run as its Gibbs campus until the county closed it in 1967.
description: Opened in 1957 by the Pinellas County Board of Public Instruction for Black students, first in Gibbs High School's building; it was regionally accredited. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1957–1965.

name: Hampton Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1966 after the Civil Rights Act of 1964 led Florida to end its separate Black junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1958–1966.

name: Jackson Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1966 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1961–1966.

kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1966 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1960–1966.

kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1966 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1960–1966.

name: Roosevelt Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1965 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: A regionally accredited Black junior college, one of the eleven Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1958–1965.

name: Rosenwald Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1966 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1958–1966.

name: Suwannee River Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1966 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1959–1966.

name: Volusia County Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1965 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1958–1965.

name: Albany State University
formerNames: Albany Bible and Manual Training Institute
description: Founded in 1903 by Joseph Winthrop Holley as the Albany Bible and Manual Training Institute, the school became a state-supported normal and agricultural college in 1917 and is now part of the University System of Georgia. After absorbing (non-HBCU) Darton State College in 2017, it is the largest historically Black institution in Georgia. Olympian Alice Coachman earned her degree there.

facts.d: Joseph Winthrop Holley, son of formerly enslaved parents, founded it in 1903.
Following its 2017 consolidation with Darton State College, it is Georgia's largest HBCU.

name: Atlanta University
affiliation: American Missionary Association; Freedmen's Bureau (early aid)
fate: Merged with Clark College in 1988 to form Clark Atlanta University.
description: Founded in 1865 with support from the American Missionary Association, Atlanta University grew from the Storrs School into a normal school and college, then from 1929–30 became an exclusively graduate institution — the first in the nation to serve African Americans — affiliated with Morehouse and Spelman. W. E. B. Du Bois taught there, and its alumni include James Weldon Johnson, Walter White, Lucy Craft Laney, Atlanta Life president Norris Herndon and Black Swan Records founder Harry Pace. Its business school trained international executives such as MTN Group's Phuthuma Nhleko and Nigeria's Oskar Ibru.

facts.d: Became an all-graduate institution around 1929–30, the first to serve African Americans.
W. E. B. Du Bois taught there, and Harry Pace (class of 1903) went into printing with him after graduating.
Phuthuma Nhleko (later CEO of MTN Group) and Oskar Ibru (later chairman of the Ibru Organisation) earned MBAs there.

name: Clark Atlanta University
description: Clark Atlanta University was formed in 1988 by the consolidation of Atlanta University (founded 1865, the first graduate institution serving African Americans) and Clark College (founded 1869 by the Methodist Freedmen's Aid Society). It is a Carnegie R2 research university in the Atlanta University Center with strong programs in business, mass media and the sciences. Its lineage produced Atlanta Life president Norris Herndon, Black Swan Records founder Harry Pace and Coca-Cola executive Carl Ware, and more recently media and music entrepreneurs such as Kenya Barris and DJ Drama.

facts.d: Atlanta University and Clark College merged in 1988 to form CAU.
Recent alumni include Black-ish creator Kenya Barris and Generation Now label co-founders DJ Drama and Don Cannon.
Diversity-management pioneer R. Roosevelt Thomas Jr. led its business school from 1979.

name: Clark College
fate: Merged with Atlanta University in 1988 to form Clark Atlanta University.
description: Founded in 1869 by the Freedmen's Aid Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church and named for Bishop Davis W. Clark, the school operated as Clark University before being renamed Clark College in 1940 when it moved next to the Atlanta University Center. It was known for journalism and teacher education. Alumni include Coca-Cola executive Carl Ware, Congressman Hank Johnson, educator Marva Collins and early Atlanta businessman Luther Judson Price.

facts.d: Founded in 1869 by the Methodist Episcopal Church's Freedmen's Aid Society.
Carl Ware (B.A., political science) rose to executive vice president of the Coca-Cola Company.

name: Fort Valley State University
formerNames: Fort Valley High and Industrial School
description: Fort Valley State College was created in 1939 by consolidating the Fort Valley High and Industrial School (chartered 1896) with the State Teachers and Agricultural College for Negroes in Forsyth. Designated Georgia's land-grant college for Black students in 1949, it became a university in 1996 and is known for agriculture and veterinary technology. Atlanta civic and business leader Thomas W. Dortch Jr. and longtime legislator and Synovus executive Calvin Smyre are alumni.

facts.d: Formed from the Fort Valley High and Industrial School and the Forsyth State Teachers and Agricultural College.
Took over Georgia's 1890 land-grant role from Savannah State in 1947–49.

name: Gammon Theological Seminary
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church / United Methodist Church
fate: Became a founding constituent seminary of the Interdenominational Theological Center (chartered 1958); ITC occupied its campus.
description: Gammon grew out of Clark University's theology department and became an independent Methodist seminary in 1883, named for benefactor Elijah H. Gammon. In 1958–59 it joined three other Black seminaries to form the Interdenominational Theological Center, which was built on the Gammon campus. Civil rights leader and SCLC president J. D. Grier earned his divinity degree there in 1956.

facts.d: Began as the theology department of Clark University (later Clark College).
One of the four seminaries that founded the ITC in 1958.

connections.label: spun out of Clark University theology dept.

name: Georgia Baptist College
kind: Private HBCU · Baptist college and grade school (defunct)
fate: Struggled financially for decades, went into foreclosure in 1937 and closed in 1956.
description: Central City College was founded in Macon in 1899 as a Black-led alternative to the white-run ABHMS schools such as Atlanta Baptist Seminary (Morehouse), spearheaded by Savannah Baptist leader Emanuel K. Love, with former Atlanta Baptist instructor William E. Holmes as first president. It operated mainly as a primary and secondary school, added a college department in 1920, was renamed Georgia Baptist College in 1938, and closed in 1956.

facts.d: Created amid disputes over white control of ABHMS schools in Georgia.
First president William E. Holmes had taught at Atlanta Baptist (Morehouse) for 25 years.

name: Haines Normal and Industrial Institute
kind: Private HBCU · Normal and industrial school (defunct)
affiliation: Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen
fate: Closed in 1949, years after founder Lucy Craft Laney's death; its site later housed Lucy C. Laney High School.
description: Lucy Craft Laney, a member of Atlanta University's first class, opened the school in Augusta in 1883 and secured backing from the northern Presbyterian Church; it was named for benefactor Francine E. H. Haines. Primarily a normal (teacher-training) and secondary institution, it trained generations of Black teachers in Georgia. Harry Pace taught there after graduating from Atlanta University, and novelist Frank Yerby graduated from it in 1933.

facts.d: Lucy Craft Laney (Atlanta University normal course, 1873) led it for 50 years.
Supported by the Presbyterian church after Laney appealed at its 1886 national convention.

sources.label: Georgia Historical Society — Haines Normal and Industrial Institute marker
New Georgia Encyclopedia — Lucy Craft Laney

name: Interdenominational Theological Center
kind: Private HBCU · Graduate theological seminary consortium
affiliation: Ecumenical (Baptist, United Methodist, AME, CME, COGIC and others)
description: The ITC was chartered in 1958 as a joint venture of four seminaries — Morehouse School of Religion (Baptist), Gammon Theological Seminary (United Methodist), Turner Theological Seminary (AME) and Phillips School of Theology (CME) — later joined by the Charles H. Mason Theological Seminary (COGIC) and others. It occupied the Gammon campus until its own buildings opened in 1961 and has trained a large share of Black clergy in the U.S.

facts.d: Founded in 1958 by Morehouse School of Religion, Gammon, Turner and Phillips seminaries.
Used the Gammon campus until its own facilities were completed in 1961.

name: Morehouse College
kind: Private HBCU · Men's liberal arts college
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society (historic); Baptist
description: Founded in 1867 in Augusta as the Augusta Institute to educate formerly enslaved men for ministry and teaching, the school moved to Atlanta in 1879 as Atlanta Baptist Seminary and took the Morehouse name in 1913. It is the nation's only historically Black college for men and the alma mater of Martin Luther King Jr. Its graduates have shaped Atlanta's Black business and political class — from Sweet Auburn newspaper founder W. A. Scott II and realtor Q. V. Williamson to Mayor Maynard Jackson, Godfather's Pizza CEO Herman Cain and filmmaker-entrepreneur Spike Lee.

facts.d: Began in 1867 at Springfield Baptist Church in Augusta before relocating to Atlanta in 1879.
Morehouse remains the only historically Black college in the U.S. exclusively for men.
Alumni include Atlanta's first Black mayor (Maynard Jackson, 1956), Sen. Raphael Warnock (1991) and a long line of Atlanta business figures.

name: Morehouse School of Medicine
formerNames: Medical Education Program at Morehouse College
description: Established in 1975 as a two-year medical education program at Morehouse College under founding dean Louis W. Sullivan, it became independent in 1981 and began awarding M.D. degrees. It focuses on primary care and health equity in underserved communities; former U.S. Surgeons General David Satcher (president) and Regina Benjamin (second graduating class) are tied to it.

facts.d: Began in 1975 as a program of Morehouse College and became independent in 1981.
Regina Benjamin was in its second graduating class; David Satcher later led the school.

name: Morris Brown College
description: Founded on January 5, 1881 by the AME Church's North Georgia Annual Conference, Morris Brown was the first educational institution in Georgia owned and operated entirely by African Americans. After losing its regional accreditation in 2002 over misuse of federal funds, it nearly closed, but regained accreditation through TRACS in 2022. Alumni include civil rights leader and businessman Hosea Williams and Atlanta's first Black woman police chief, Beverly Harvard.

facts.d: First Georgia educational institution founded and run entirely by African Americans.
Unaccredited from 2003 to 2022; now accredited by the Transnational Association of Christian Colleges and Schools.
Payne College of Cuthbert, Georgia became part of Morris Brown in 1912.

name: Paine College
affiliation: Christian Methodist Episcopal Church; United Methodist Church
description: Paine was founded on November 1, 1882 as a joint project of the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church and the white Methodist Episcopal Church, South — an unusual biracial partnership in the post-Reconstruction South. After SACS revoked its regional accreditation in 2016 amid financial problems, it is now accredited by TRACS. Alumni include novelist Frank Yerby, SCLC co-founder Joseph Lowery and Georgia Labor Commissioner Michael Thurmond.

facts.d: Founded by the CME Church together with the Methodist Episcopal Church, South.
Lost SACS accreditation in 2016; now accredited by TRACS.

name: Payne College (Cuthbert)
fate: Became part of Morris Brown University on June 5, 1912.
description: Payne College was a small AME-affiliated school founded in 1879 in Cuthbert, in southwest Georgia. It operated until 1912, when it was absorbed into Morris Brown in Atlanta. It is distinct from Paine College in Augusta.

facts.d: On June 5, 1912 it became part of Morris Brown University.

name: Savannah State University
formerNames: Georgia State Industrial College for Colored Youth
description: Created by the Georgia General Assembly on November 26, 1890 under the Second Morrill Act as the Georgia State Industrial College for Colored Youth, it is the oldest public HBCU in Georgia. Founding president Richard R. Wright Sr. led it for three decades before founding a bank in Philadelphia. It served as Georgia's Black land-grant college until 1947. Alumni include civil rights leader W. W. Law and Pro Football Hall of Famer turned media entrepreneur Shannon Sharpe.

facts.d: Chartered November 26, 1890; classes moved to Savannah in October 1891.
First president Richard R. Wright Sr. later founded Citizens and Southern Bank and Trust Co. in Philadelphia.

name: Spelman College
kind: Private HBCU · Women's liberal arts college
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society (historic); Baptist
description: Founded in 1881 in the basement of Atlanta's Friendship Baptist Church by New England missionaries Sophia B. Packard and Harriet E. Giles as the Atlanta Baptist Female Seminary, it was renamed for the Spelman family (in-laws of John D. Rockefeller, its early benefactor) and became Spelman College in 1924. It is consistently ranked the top HBCU and is the nation's leading producer of Black women who go on to STEM doctorates. Alumnae include Walgreens CEO Rosalind Brewer, Children's Defense Fund founder Marian Wright Edelman and Stacey Abrams.

facts.d: John D. Rockefeller's support led the school to adopt the name of his wife Laura Spelman's family in 1884.
Rosalind Brewer (chemistry, 1984) became CEO of Sam's Club and Walgreens Boots Alliance and later chaired Spelman's board.
One of only two remaining historically Black colleges for women (with Bennett College).

name: State Teachers and Agricultural College for Negroes
kind: Public HBCU · Teachers and agricultural college (defunct)
affiliation: American Missionary Association (early funding); University System of Georgia (from 1932)
formerNames: School of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts for the Training of Negroes
fate: Closed in 1938 and consolidated into the new Fort Valley State College in 1939; its campus became the Hubbard Training School.
description: Founded in 1902 by Rev. William Merida Hubbard as the Forsyth Normal and Industrial School with early help from the American Missionary Association, it was accredited in 1918 as Georgia's first vocational school for Black students. It became a public teachers college in 1931 and one of three Black public colleges added to the University System of Georgia in 1932, before the state merged it into Fort Valley State in 1939.

facts.d: Accredited in 1918 as the first vocational training school for African Americans in Georgia.
Consolidated into Fort Valley State College in 1939.

sources.label: Wikipedia — State Teachers and Agricultural College for Negroes (Georgia)

name: Western University
fate: Lost funding in the Great Depression and competition for students; closed in 1943. Only a John Brown statue remains of the campus.
description: Began as the Quindaro Freedman's School in the free-state river town of Quindaro, an Underground Railroad stop, and became Western University in 1881 when the AME Church took it over. Its music department was celebrated: alumni included choral pioneer Eva Jessye and singer-actress Etta Moten Barnett.

facts.d: The only HBCU in Kansas history; state funds supported its industrial department.
Will Marion Cook taught there; Eva Jessye, Nora Douglas Holt and Etta Moten Barnett studied there.
Only the John Brown statue in front of the former Ward Hall survives.

sources.label: Community Voice — Quindaro Freedman's School was Kansas's HBCU

name: Eckstein Norton Institute
affiliation: Black Baptist leadership (founded by William J. Simmons and Charles H. Parrish)
fate: Merged in 1912 into the new Lincoln Institute (a segregated boarding high school) after Kentucky's 1904 Day Law.
description: Founded in 1890 by Dr. William J. Simmons and Rev. Charles H. Parrish, the institute taught shorthand, telegraphy, printing, cabinetmaking and music to Black Kentuckians—an explicitly vocational and commercial curriculum. It merged into Lincoln Institute in Shelby County in 1912.

facts.d: Courses included shorthand, telegraphy and printing.

name: Kentucky State University
formerNames: State Normal School for Colored Persons
Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons
Kentucky State Industrial College for Colored Persons
description: Chartered in 1886 as the State Normal School for Colored Persons, Kentucky State became the commonwealth's Black land-grant college and a university in 1972. Alumni include National Urban League leader Whitney M. Young Jr., Pulitzer-winning Ebony photographer Moneta Sleet Jr., and Thailand's first female prime minister Yingluck Shinawatra, formerly CEO of telecom giant AIS.

facts.d: Yingluck Shinawatra earned an MPA here in 1991 before running Advanced Info Service and becoming Thai prime minister.
Whitney M. Young Jr. (1941) led the National Urban League into corporate partnerships in the 1960s.

name: Louisville Municipal College
fate: Closed in 1951 when the University of Louisville desegregated and absorbed it.
description: Created as the University of Louisville's segregated Black campus after Black voters forced a 1925 bond compromise, it opened in 1931 on the foreclosed Simmons University site. It was folded into the University of Louisville in 1951. Alumni include Kentucky's first Black female state senator, Georgia Davis Powers.

facts.d: Black opposition sank a 1920 university bond; the 1925 compromise reserved about 10% of proceeds for a Black college.

name: Louisville National Medical College
affiliation: Independent; later affiliated with State University (Simmons)
fate: Closed/merged around 1912 in the Flexner era; Wikipedia's Simmons entry says it merged into Simmons.
description: A historically Black medical school founded in 1888 in Louisville; its first graduate was a woman. It was one of the Black medical schools that did not survive the reforms following the 1910 Flexner Report.

facts.d: Wikipedia notes the school's first graduate was a woman.

name: Simmons College of Kentucky
kind: Private HBCU · Liberal arts & Bible college
affiliation: General Association of Colored Baptists in Kentucky / National Baptist tradition
description: Founded in 1879 by Kentucky's Black Baptists and built up by president William J. Simmons, the school became a full university offering law and medicine before losing its campus to foreclosure in 1930. It survived as Simmons Bible College, returned to its original campus under Kevin Cosby in 2006, and was recognized as the nation's 107th HBCU.

facts.d: Lost its property in 1930 (the site then housed Louisville Municipal College) and moved back to it in 2006.
Louisville National Medical College merged into the university in the early 1900s.

name: Coleman College
affiliation: Black Baptist (Springfield Baptist Association; American Baptist Home Mission Societies funding)
fate: Crippled by a 1926 fire and founder Oliver Coleman's 1927 death, the Gibsland school closed (dates given as 1937 or 1944), moved to Shreveport as a Bible college and faded by the mid-1950s.
description: Begun in 1887 by Oliver Lewis Coleman with eight students at Palestine Baptist Church in Gibsland, Coleman College is described as the first Black institution of higher learning in North Louisiana. Local farmers donated crops and lumber; it was Grambling's chief early athletic rival.

facts.d: Often called the first college for African Americans in North Louisiana.
The campus became Gibsland-Coleman High School; a marker was unveiled in 2014.

connections.label: supported by local Black Baptist association

name: Dillard University
affiliation: United Methodist Church; United Church of Christ
description: Chartered June 6, 1930 through the union of Straight College (American Missionary Association) and New Orleans University (Methodist Freedmen's Aid Society), Dillard carries a lineage back to 1868–69. Graduates include Brown University president Ruth Simmons, corporate executive Joyce Roché and musician-label founder Harold Battiste.

facts.t: A merger of two Reconstruction schools.
facts.d: Straight College and New Orleans University jointly chartered Dillard in 1930.
P.B.S. Pinchback and Louis A. Martinet, organizer of the Plessy challenge, studied law at Straight.
Joyce Roché ('70) became president of Carson Inc. and served on the AT&T board.

connections.label: via New Orleans University (Freedmen's Aid Society)

name: Grambling State University
affiliation: State of Louisiana (University of Louisiana System)
formerNames: North Louisiana Agricultural and Industrial School
Louisiana Negro Normal and Industrial Institute
description: Opened November 1, 1901 under founder Charles P. Adams as the Colored Industrial and Agricultural School, Grambling became nationally famous through coach Eddie Robinson's 57-year football dynasty. Its alumni run from Packers great-turned-broadcasting owner Willie Davis to music executive Tina Davis, CPA firm leader Wayne McConnell and rapper-entrepreneur E-40.

facts.d: Robinson coached football 1941–1997 and won 408 games.
Hall of Famers include Willie Davis, Buck Buchanan, Willie Brown and Charlie Joiner; Doug Williams was Super Bowl XXII MVP.
Earned university status when graduate education programs were added.

name: Leland College
affiliation: Baptist (Christian college founded by Holbrook Chamberlain)
fate: After a 1915 hurricane wrecked University Hall the New Orleans campus was sold; it reopened near Baker in 1923 but, never accredited and short of funds, closed in 1960.
description: Founded in 1870 by Brooklyn philanthropist Holbrook Chamberlain on St. Charles Avenue in New Orleans, Leland admitted students regardless of race. Its most famous graduate, Eddie Robinson (1941), became Grambling's legendary football coach.

facts.d: Original campus sat across from Audubon Park.
Robinson earned his bachelor's degree at Leland in 1941.

name: Luther College (New Orleans)
kind: Private HBCU · Lutheran normal school & seminary
affiliation: Evangelical Lutheran Synodical Conference (Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod)
fate: The Synodical Conference closed it in 1925 (some sources say 1932), citing the failed seminary and high building costs; funds went to Alabama Lutheran College in Selma.
description: Founded in 1903 by the Evangelical Lutheran Synodical Conference as a secondary school, normal school and seminary for African Americans, Luther College was the sister school of Immanuel Lutheran College in North Carolina.

facts.d: The seminary closed in 1910 after graduating one student.
Resources were diverted to Alabama Lutheran College (now Concordia College Alabama).

name: New Orleans University
fate: Merged with Straight College in 1930 to form Dillard University.
description: Established July 8, 1868 as Union Normal School by the Methodist Freedmen's Aid Society, it grew into New Orleans University, whose Flint Medical College (closed 1911) gave rise to Flint-Goodridge Hospital. It merged with Straight College in 1930 to form Dillard.

facts.d: Flint Medical College closed in 1911; Flint-Goodridge Hospital continued nurse training.
Alumnus John W. E. Bowen Sr. (1878) was among the first African Americans to earn a Ph.D.

name: Southern University and A&M College
affiliation: State of Louisiana (Southern University System); 1890 land-grant
description: Chartered by the Louisiana General Assembly in 1880 in New Orleans and opened in 1881 with 12 students, Southern became the state's Black land-grant college in 1890 and moved to Scotlandville above Baton Rouge in 1914. It is the flagship of the only HBCU system in the U.S. Alumni include Zenith Bank founder Jim Ovia, music executive Randy Jackson and NASA engineer-turned-founder Morgan Watson.

facts.d: Early classes met in the former Israel Sinai Temple on Calliope Street, New Orleans.
Relocated to Scott's Bluff in Scotlandville.
A 1974 special legislative session created the Southern University System.

name: Southern University at New Orleans
description: Created by Act 28 of a 1956 extraordinary legislative session as a branch of Southern University, SUNO opened in Pontchartrain Park in 1959 and became a center of student civil-rights activism, home to CORE leader Oretha Castle Haley. All 11 buildings were damaged by Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005.

facts.d: Established September 4, 1956; opened September 21, 1959.
All 11 Park Campus buildings were damaged in 2005.
Only Louisiana institution offering an advanced degree in museum studies.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Southern University at New Orleans

name: Southern University at Shreveport
description: Southern University at Shreveport opened September 19, 1967 as a junior college of the Southern University System, offering associate degrees, technical diplomas and certificates in allied health, business and STEM to northwest Louisiana.

facts.d: Instruction began September 19, 1967.
Divisions in Allied Health & Nursing and in Business, Science, Technology, Engineering and Math.

name: Straight University
fate: Renamed Straight College in 1915 and merged with New Orleans University in 1930 to form Dillard University.
description: Founded by the American Missionary Association in 1868–69, Straight ran a law department that trained Reconstruction-era leaders including Governor P.B.S. Pinchback and Louis A. Martinet, publisher of The Crusader and organizer of the Comité des Citoyens behind Plessy v. Ferguson. Businessman Walter L. Cohen, founder of People's Life Insurance, also studied there.

facts.d: Martinet earned his law degree in 1876; Pinchback graduated in 1885.
Merged into Dillard in 1930.

sources.label: Dillard University — Distinguished alumni (Straight College entries)

name: Xavier University of Louisiana
affiliation: Catholic Church (Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament)
formerNames: Xavier University Preparatory School (1915 high school)
description: The only historically Black Catholic university in the U.S., Xavier was founded by St. Katharine Drexel and the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament (high school 1915, college 1925). Led for 47 years by alumnus Norman C. Francis, it is a leading producer of Black pharmacists and medical school applicants. Business alumni include Harold Doley, the first Black individual to buy a New York Stock Exchange seat.

facts.d: St. Katharine Drexel founded it through the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament.
Its College of Pharmacy trained entrepreneurs such as Lexington's Zirl Palmer, first Black Rexall franchise owner.
Alumnus Norman C. Francis was president 1968–2015.

connections.label: founded by St. Katharine Drexel & Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament

name: Bowie State University
affiliation: Baltimore Association for the Moral and Educational Improvement of the Colored People (founding); University System of Maryland
formerNames: Baltimore Normal School for Colored Teachers
Maryland Normal and Industrial School at Bowie
description: Maryland's oldest HBCU, it was started in 1865 by the Baltimore Association for the Moral and Educational Improvement of the Colored People as a teacher-training school meeting in a Baltimore church. It moved to a 187-acre Prince George's County farm in 1910 and grew from a normal school into a comprehensive university with a College of Business. In 1992 it became the first HBCU to run graduate programs overseas.

facts.d: Founded January 9, 1865; first classes met at the African Baptist Church in Baltimore.
Relocated in 1910 to a 187-acre farm in Prince George's County, today's campus.
In 1992 it became the first HBCU to offer graduate programs abroad for U.S. military personnel.
MacKenzie Scott gave $25 million in 2020 and $50 million in 2025, the largest gift in its history.

name: Coppin State University
affiliation: Baltimore City School Board (founding); University System of Maryland
description: Begun in 1900 as a one-year teacher-training course at Baltimore's Colored High School (later Douglass High), it was named in 1926 for Institute for Colored Youth educator Fanny Jackson Coppin. It joined the state system in 1950, moved to West North Avenue in 1952 and broadened beyond teacher education in 1963. It is an urban, largely commuter university in West Baltimore.

facts.d: Renamed in 1926 for Fanny Jackson Coppin, longtime principal of Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth (today's Cheyney).
Four-year B.S. by 1938, first B.A. in 1967, university status in 2004.
In 2022 it offered free tuition to graduates of Philadelphia's Fanny Jackson Coppin School.

connections.label: named for ICY principal Fanny Jackson Coppin

name: Morgan State University
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church (founding); State of Maryland since 1939
description: Founded in 1867 by the Methodist Episcopal Church as the Centenary Biblical Institute to train men for the ministry, it became Morgan College in 1890 and was bought by the State of Maryland in 1939. It is Maryland's largest HBCU and a designated public urban research university. Its Earl G. Graves School of Business and Management is named for the Black Enterprise founder, one of its best-known alumni.

facts.d: Began as a Methodist Episcopal seminary (1867), renamed for board chair Lyttleton Morgan in 1890, and became public in 1939 when Maryland purchased it.

facts.t: Earl G. Graves School of Business.
facts.d: The AACSB-accredited business school is named for alumnus Earl G. Graves Sr.; its new building opened in fall 2015.
Former UPS executive Calvin E. Tyler Jr., who left Morgan in 1963 for lack of money, and his wife Tina committed $20 million in 2021 — the largest alumni gift in Morgan's history.

facts.t: Parent of an Eastern Shore campus.
facts.d: Morgan College's Delaware Conference Academy at Princess Anne grew into today's University of Maryland Eastern Shore.

sources.label: Morgan State — Morgan State is Black History!

name: University of Maryland Eastern Shore
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church, Delaware Conference (founding); 1890 land-grant; University System of Maryland
formerNames: Eastern Shore Branch of the Maryland Agricultural College
description: Opened September 13, 1886, with nine students in a converted farmhouse as the Delaware Conference Academy, a Methodist preparatory branch of Morgan College. Maryland used it to satisfy the Second Morrill Act's requirement for a Black land-grant college, and it passed from church to state control about fifty years after opening. It became the University of Maryland Eastern Shore in 1970.

facts.d: Founded as a preparatory school for Baltimore's Centenary Biblical Institute / Morgan College.
Because Black students were barred from the College Park agricultural college, Maryland partnered with Morgan to provide the 1890 land-grant college on the Lower Eastern Shore.
UMES was a founding member of the Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference in 1970 and produced Hall of Famer Art Shell.
MacKenzie Scott gave $20 million (2020) and $38 million (2025), the largest single gift in UMES history.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of Maryland Eastern Shore

connections.label: began as Morgan College's preparatory branch

name: Pensole Lewis College of Business & Design
description: Violet T. Lewis, a Wilberforce-trained businesswoman, opened Lewis Business College in Indianapolis in 1928 on a $50 loan and opened a Detroit branch around 1938–39; it was Michigan's only HBCU. After losing accreditation and a long decline it closed around 2013–2015, then was revived in 2021–22 by designer D'Wayne Edwards as Pensole Lewis College — described as the first closed HBCU ever to reopen.

facts.d: Violet T. Lewis opened the school in January 1928 in Indianapolis.
Sources differ on whether the Education Department designated it an HBCU in 1957 or 1987.
Rebranded in 2021 and re-established under Michigan legislation; was pursuing new accreditation in partnership with the College for Creative Studies.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Pensole Lewis College of Business and Design
TPInsights — First closed HBCU to reopen

name: George R. Smith College
fate: Its building burned on April 26, 1925 and it never reopened; its assets were merged into Philander Smith College in 1933.
description: A Methodist college for Black students in Sedalia, Missouri, named for the town's founder. It operated for three decades until a 1925 fire destroyed it.

facts.d: Burned April 26, 1925.
Merged into Philander Smith College (Little Rock) in 1933.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Harris–Stowe State University
description: Formed in 1954 when St. Louis's white Harris Teachers College (1857) merged with Stowe Teachers College, the city's Black teachers college, as the schools desegregated. It is a public HBCU in downtown St. Louis focused on education and business; alumni include federal judge Charles Shaw and anchorman Julius Hunter.

facts.d: HBCU status descends from Stowe Teachers College, merged in 1954.
An African American business leaders council has raised over $400,000 in scholarships for its business program.

sources.label: NewsOne — HBCU spotlight: Harris-Stowe State University

name: Lincoln University of Missouri
description: Founded in 1866 by Black Union veterans of the 62nd and 65th U.S. Colored Infantry, who pooled their pay to start Lincoln Institute. It became Missouri's 1890 land-grant school and was at the center of Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938). Business alumni include restaurant franchise mogul Valerie Daniels-Carter, barbecue king Ollie Gates and Walmart heiress Ann Walton Kroenke.

facts.d: Soldiers of the 62nd and 65th U.S. Colored Infantry funded the school in 1866.
Black Enterprise identifies nursing graduate Ann Walton Kroenke, a billionaire Walmart heir, as the wealthiest HBCU graduate.
Valerie Daniels-Carter (1978) keynoted the 2026 Founders' Day.

name: Stowe Teachers College
fate: Merged with Harris Teachers College in 1954 to form Harris-Stowe (now Harris–Stowe State University).
description: St. Louis's normal school for Black teachers, begun in connection with Sumner High School and later named for Harriet Beecher Stowe. Its 1954 merger with the white Harris Teachers College is the source of Harris–Stowe's HBCU status.

facts.d: Combined with Harris Teachers College as St. Louis schools desegregated.

name: Western Baptist Bible College
affiliation: Black Baptist General Association of Missouri
description: Founded in 1890 by African American Baptist ministers in Independence, Missouri, it moved to Macon and then to Kansas City (1921) and calls itself the first Christian institution west of the Mississippi founded exclusively by Black people. It closed in the Depression (1935–36) and reopened as Western Seminary in 1937; it is not on the federal HBCU list.

facts.d: Described as the 'first and only Christian institution west of the Mississippi River founded by blacks exclusively.'

sources.label: African American Historic Textbook of KC — Western Baptist Bible College

name: Alcorn State University
description: Founded in 1871 on the former Oakland College campus with Senator Hiram Revels as first president, Alcorn was the first Black land-grant college in the United States. Its alumni include insurance and banking pioneer Joseph Edison Walker (Universal Life, Tri-State Bank), Medgar and Charles Evers, Alex Haley and Steve McNair.

facts.d: Land-grant from its founding in 1871.
The first Black U.S. senator was Alcorn's founding president.
Alumnus J. E. Walker co-founded Memphis's Universal Life Insurance (1923) and Tri-State Bank (1946).

name: Coahoma Community College
formerNames: Coahoma Junior College and Agricultural High School
description: Grew out of the Coahoma County Agricultural High School (1924) and added a junior college in 1949; renamed Coahoma Community College in 1989. It serves the Mississippi Delta from a rural campus near Clarksdale.

facts.d: Began as a 1924 county agricultural high school for Black students.
Became Coahoma Community College in 1989.

name: Hinds Community College–Utica
description: Founded in 1903 as Utica Normal and Industrial Institute by Tuskegee graduate William H. Holtzclaw on the Booker T. Washington model, it became Utica Junior College and was merged into Hinds Junior College in 1982 under a federal desegregation court order. The Utica campus retains its HBCU identity.

facts.d: Founder William H. Holtzclaw was a Tuskegee graduate who replicated its industrial-education model.
Merged with Hinds in 1982 as part of a class-action racial discrimination case.

connections.label: founded by Tuskegee graduate William H. Holtzclaw

name: J. P. Campbell College
fate: Seized by the state through eminent domain and closed in 1964; scholars link the decision to its role in the Jackson civil-rights movement.
description: Founded in Vicksburg in 1890 by the AME Church and moved to Jackson in 1898, Campbell College admitted students expelled from other schools for civil-rights activism before the state took its land in 1964.

facts.d: Admitted students expelled for civil-rights activism.
The state acquired the campus in 1964.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Jackson State University
affiliation: Thurgood Marshall College Fund; American Baptist Home Mission Society (founder)
description: Founded in Natchez in 1877 by the American Baptist Home Mission Society, it moved to Jackson in 1882 and became a state school in 1940. JSU is Mississippi's largest HBCU and its urban research university; alumni include Walter Payton, Secretary of Education Rod Paige, Rep. Bennie Thompson and Jackson Advocate founder Percy Greene.

facts.d: Opened as Natchez Seminary (1877) under the American Baptist Home Mission Society.
Police killed two people at Alexander Hall in May 1970, days after Kent State.
Walter Payton parlayed his career into heavy-equipment, racing and restaurant ventures.

name: Mary Holmes College
affiliation: Presbyterian Church (Board of Missions for Freedmen)
fate: Lost SACS accreditation in 2002 and closed in March 2005 after failing to attract enough students and funds.
description: Opened in 1892 in Jackson as Mary Holmes Seminary — conceived by missionary Rev. Mead Holmes and his daughter Mary — under the Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen, later relocating to West Point. It became a junior college in 1959 and closed in 2005.

facts.d: Named for Mary Emilie Holmes, who with her father Mead Holmes conceived the school.
Lost accreditation in 2002; closed 2005.

connections.label: funded and overseen by the Board

name: Mississippi Industrial College
fate: Enrollment fell after Mississippi's community colleges desegregated; the campus closed in 1982 and was bought by Rust College in 2008.
description: Founded in 1905 by the Mississippi Conference of the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church under Bishop Elias Cottrell, MIC educated generations of north Mississippi teachers and CME clergy. Its campus is on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.d: Bishop Elias Cottrell, born enslaved, led its founding.
Listed on the National Register in 1980; acquired by Rust College in 2008.

connections.label: founded by the CME Mississippi Conference

name: Mississippi Valley State University
description: Created by the legislature in 1946 and opened in 1950 in the Delta as Mississippi Vocational College — partly to keep Black students out of white state schools — MVSU became a university in 1974. It is best known for Jerry Rice and the record-setting 1984 Delta Devils offense.

facts.d: Legislation signed April 5, 1946; opened 1950.
The Hall of Fame receiver played at Valley 1981–84.

name: Mount Hermon Female Seminary
fate: The AMA closed it in 1924 because it already operated Tougaloo College nearby.
description: Founded in 1875 by Sarah Ann Dickey on the Mount Holyoke model to educate Black women, it was supported by the Slater Fund and taken over by the American Missionary Association after Dickey's death in 1903.

facts.d: Dickey patterned it on her alma mater.
The AMA consolidated its Mississippi work at Tougaloo.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Natchez College
affiliation: Mississippi Black Baptist State Missionary Convention
fate: Stopped granting bachelor's degrees in the 1960s and, as Natchez Junior College, closed in 1989 (some lists give 1993).
description: Founded in 1884 by the Baptist State Missionary Convention under George W. Gayles, Natchez College trained Black teachers and ministers in southwest Mississippi; Booker T. Washington visited in 1908. Alumni include Mound Bayou banker Eugene P. Booze and author Anne Moody.

facts.d: Founded through the Baptist State Missionary Convention led by George W. Gayles.
Alumnus Eugene P. Booze co-founded the Bank of Mound Bayou (1904).

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

connections.label: founded by Mississippi's Black Baptist convention

name: Okolona College
affiliation: American Church Institute for Negroes (Episcopal), from 1921
fate: Closed in 1965 amid financial difficulties (about 60% of its budget came from donations) as public options opened after the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
description: Founded in 1902 by Wallace A. Battle on the Tuskegee industrial model, Okolona joined the Episcopal Church's American Church Institute for Negroes in 1921 and was reorganized in 1933 into a high school and two-year junior college.

facts.d: Battle, influenced by Booker T. Washington, taught agriculture, mechanical arts and teacher training.
Teacher Ulysses S. Baskin was murdered on commencement day amid racist harassment.

connections.label: American Church Institute for Negroes affiliate from 1921

name: Prentiss Institute
fate: Phased out lower grades after 1959 and closed in 1989; the campus is now a museum and historic district.
description: Founded in 1907 by Jonas Edward and Bertha LaBranche Johnson in a former plantation house, Prentiss combined academic and industrial training, became a junior college in 1931 and enrolled about 700 students by 1957.

facts.d: The Johnsons lived in the plantation house where classes began.
Received Rosenwald funding and ran a Heifer International dairy program.

name: Rust College
description: Founded in 1866 by Northern missionaries of the Methodist Episcopal Church's Freedmen's Aid Society, Rust is Mississippi's oldest private HBCU. Its early alumni include journalist Ida B. Wells and Mound Bayou banker Charles Banks; later graduates include Las Vegas pain-medicine entrepreneur Godwin Maduka and Hi Records chief Willie Mitchell.

facts.d: Shaw University (1870) became Rust University in 1892 to avoid confusion with Shaw University in Raleigh; Rust College from 1915.
Charles Banks (Bank of Mound Bayou) and Ida B. Wells (Free Speech) attended.
Bought the closed Mississippi Industrial College campus across the street in 2008.

connections.label: founded by the Freedmen's Aid Society

name: Saints Junior College
fate: The junior college faded after president Arenia Mallory's death in 1977; the academy closed in 2006 as the Delta's population declined.
description: Founded in 1918 by COGIC founder Charles H. Mason as the Saints Industrial and Literary School, it grew under Arenia Mallory (1926–1977) into a respected academy and junior college in Holmes County.

facts.d: A ministry of St. Paul's Church of God in Christ, Lexington.
Mallory (a Jackson State alumna) led it for 51 years.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Southern Christian Institute
fate: Merged into Tougaloo College in 1954; its Edwards campus, renamed Mt. Beulah, later hosted civil-rights organizations.
description: Founded in 1882 by the Disciples of Christ to educate African Americans, SCI merged with Tougaloo in 1954 — the source of Tougaloo's Disciples of Christ affiliation.

facts.d: Founded by the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ).
Joined Tougaloo College.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

connections.label: founded by the Disciples of Christ

name: Tougaloo College
affiliation: American Missionary Association; United Church of Christ; Disciples of Christ; UNCF
