description: Established in 1869 by the American Missionary Association on a former plantation north of Jackson, Tougaloo was the 'cradle' of Mississippi's civil-rights movement, hosting the 1963 Woolworth sit-in organizers. Alumni include Justice Reuben V. Anderson, Rep. Bennie Thompson, author Anne Moody and Jackson Medical Mall founder Aaron Shirley.

facts.d: The AMA bought the plantation land to educate freedpeople.
The Disciples of Christ's Southern Christian Institute merged into Tougaloo in 1954.
Tougaloo students led the 1963 Jackson Woolworth's sit-in.

name: Barber Memorial College
affiliation: Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen
fate: Merged into Scotia Women's College in Concord, NC, in 1930 to form Barber–Scotia.
description: A Presbyterian school for Black girls founded in Anniston, Alabama, in 1896 through Margaret M. Barber's gift. In 1930 it merged with Scotia Women's College in North Carolina, giving Barber–Scotia its name.

facts.d: Established with funds from Margaret M. Barber as a memorial.
Combined with Scotia Women's College to form Barber–Scotia Junior College.

name: Barber–Scotia College
fate: Lost SACS accreditation in 2004; operating with ~100 students and pursuing TRACS accreditation as of 2026.
description: Founded in 1867 by Rev. Luke Dorland as Scotia Seminary to train Black women as teachers, it absorbed Alabama's Barber Memorial College in 1930. Its most famous alumna is Mary McLeod Bethune. Accreditation was revoked in 2004; the college regained tax-exempt status in 2026 and is rebuilding.

facts.d: Mary McLeod Bethune graduated from Scotia Seminary before founding what became Bethune-Cookman University.
Merged with Barber Memorial College (Anniston, Ala., founded 1896) to form Barber–Scotia.
SACS revoked accreditation after degrees were awarded to adult students who had not met requirements.

sources.label: WFAE — Barber-Scotia College regains tax-exempt status (Jan. 2026)

name: Bennett College
affiliation: United Methodist Church (Freedmen's Aid Society); UNCF; TRACS-accredited since 2023
description: Founded in 1873 as a coeducational normal school in the basement of Greensboro's St. Matthews Methodist Church, it was named for New York donor Lyman Bennett and became a women's college in 1926. Bennett women organized a 1937 theater boycott and helped plan the 1960 sit-ins. After losing SACSCOC accreditation in 2019 it rebuilt and won TRACS accreditation in 2023.

facts.d: One of only two historically Black women's colleges (with Spelman).
SACSCOC withdrew accreditation over finances in 2019; the college raised emergency funds and was accredited by TRACS in April 2023.
Alumna I. Patricia Henry ('69) became the first African American woman to manage a major U.S. brewery.

sources.label: WUNC — Bennett College files federal complaint (May 2026)

name: Brick Junior College
affiliation: American Missionary Association; United Church of Christ
formerNames: Joseph K. Brick Agricultural, Industrial and Normal School
fate: Closed in 1933 as Depression-era cuts slashed AMA funding and enrollment; the campus became the Brick Rural Life School and later the UCC's Franklinton Center.
description: Opened in 1895 by the American Missionary Association on land given by Brooklyn widow Julia Brick, under principal Thomas S. Inborden. It added a junior college in 1925–26 and closed in 1933. Carolina Times publisher Louis Austin finished his schooling there.

facts.d: Named for Joseph Keasbey Brick; opened Oct. 1, 1895 with 54 students.
The college division opened with 24 students before the Depression forced closure.

sources.label: NC DNCR — Brick School historical marker (E-90)

name: Elizabeth City State University
affiliation: University of North Carolina System; Thurgood Marshall College Fund
formerNames: State Colored Normal School at Elizabeth City
description: Created by the General Assembly in 1891 as a normal school for Black teachers in northeastern North Carolina, led for 37 years by Shaw graduate Peter Weddick Moore. Today it serves a largely rural northeastern North Carolina region and offers programs including aviation science and pharmacy.

facts.d: First leader Peter Weddick Moore earned his A.B. at Shaw University in 1887.
Serves a largely rural 21-county region of northeastern North Carolina.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Shaw University (alumni incl. P. W. Moore)

name: Fayetteville State University
affiliation: University of North Carolina System; Thurgood Marshall College Fund; Freedmen's Bureau origins
description: Founded in 1867 as the Howard School on land bought by seven Black Fayetteville men, with Freedmen's Bureau support named for Gen. Oliver O. Howard. It became the State Colored Normal School in 1877, one of the earliest state-supported normal schools for Black teachers in the South, and today serves the Fort Bragg military community.

facts.d: Matthew N. Leary, Andrew J. Chesnutt, Robert Simmons, George Grainger, Thomas Lomax, Nelson Carter and David A. Bryant bought the land and formed a self-perpetuating board.
Designated the State Colored Normal School in 1877 to train Black teachers for the state.

name: Immanuel Lutheran College
kind: Private HBCU · High school, junior college & seminary (Lutheran)
affiliation: Evangelical Lutheran Synodical Conference (Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod)
fate: Closed June 30, 1961 when the Synodical Conference integrated Black ministerial training into Missouri Synod schools; the state bought the campus for $239,000 as N.C. A&T's East Campus.
description: Founded in Concord in 1903 and moved to Greensboro in 1905, it trained Black Lutheran pastors and teachers through a high school, an accredited junior college and a seminary. Its campus next to N.C. A&T was sold to the state when it closed in 1961.

facts.d: Operated a four-year seminary alongside the junior college.
North Carolina bought the campus for $239,000; it became A&T's East Campus.

connections.label: campus sold to become A&T's East Campus, 1961

name: Johnson C. Smith University
description: Founded in 1867 by the Catawba Presbytery as Biddle Memorial Institute with a $1,400 gift from Mary D. Biddle, it was renamed in 1923 for Johnson Crayne Smith after his widow Jane Berry Smith's gifts. It was a 1944 founding member of UNCF and benefited from the Duke Endowment from 1924; it played the first Black college football game (vs. Livingstone, 1892).

facts.d: Biddle University played Livingstone College in Salisbury in December 1892, the first intercollegiate football game between Black colleges.
Named in James B. Duke's 1924 indenture as a beneficiary of the Duke Endowment.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of Johnson C. Smith University alumni

name: Kittrell College
fate: Closed after its last graduating class in 1975 amid unpaid debts, a federal-funds investigation and campus fires; the campus became a Job Corps center in 1979.
description: Chartered in 1886 by the AME Church's North Carolina Conference as Kittrell Normal and Industrial School in Vance County, it served rural Black students as a two-year college for nearly 90 years. Durham business founder W. G. Pearson was a trustee.

facts.d: Authorized by the AME North Carolina Conference under Bishop William Fisher Dickerson in 1885.
The campus has housed the Kittrell Job Corps Center since 1979.

name: Leonard Medical School
kind: Private HBCU professional school · Medicine (Shaw University)
affiliation: Shaw University; American Baptist Home Mission Society
fate: Closed in 1918 under financial strain from trying to meet Flexner Report standards.
description: The medical school of Shaw University, housed in Leonard Hall (completed 1881, named for donor Judson Wade Leonard), is described as the first four-year medical school in the country open to African Americans. In 36 years it graduated nearly 400 physicians, several of whom co-founded North Carolina Mutual, Mechanics & Farmers Bank and Lincoln Hospital in Durham.

facts.d: Awarded its first medical degrees in 1886 to six men.
Alumni Aaron M. Moore, Stanford L. Warren and Manassa T. Pope founded insurers, drugstores and a bank alongside their practices.
Closed in 1918, one of several Black medical schools lost after the 1910 Flexner Report.

connections.label: medical school of Shaw University; closed 1918

name: Livingstone College
affiliation: African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church; UNCF
description: Founded in 1879 by the AME Zion Church as Zion Wesley Institute in Concord, it moved to Salisbury in 1882 and was renamed for David Livingstone in 1887 under president Joseph C. Price. Alumni include Harlem real-estate pioneer Philip A. Payton Jr., UNCF architect William J. Trent Jr., and educator J. E. K. Aggrey.

facts.d: Joseph C. Price raised funds in England to establish the school before moving it to Salisbury.
Alumnus William J. Trent Jr. (1930) ran the United Negro College Fund from 1944 to 1964.

name: North Carolina A&T State University
affiliation: Second Morrill Act (1890) land-grant; University of North Carolina System; Thurgood Marshall College Fund
formerNames: Agricultural and Mechanical College for the Colored Race
Negro Agricultural and Technical College of North Carolina
Agricultural and Technical College of North Carolina
description: Chartered by the North Carolina General Assembly in 1891 as the Agricultural and Mechanical College for the Colored Race, it began as an annex of Shaw University in Raleigh before moving to Greensboro in 1892. It is the largest HBCU by enrollment and a leading producer of Black engineers. Its students launched the 1960 Woolworth sit-ins, and its business school is named for Merck executive and alumnus Willie A. Deese.

facts.d: Opened in Raleigh in 1891 with four teachers and 37 students as an annex of Shaw University, then moved to Greensboro in 1892.
On Feb. 1, 1960, freshmen Ezell Blair Jr. (Jibreel Khazan), Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil and David Richmond sat in at the Greensboro Woolworth lunch counter, sparking a national sit-in movement.
In 2019 A&T named its College of Business and Economics for Willie A. Deese ('77) — the first college at the university to carry a donor's name.

sources.label: Wikipedia — North Carolina A&T State University

connections.label: began as an annex of Shaw University, 1891

name: North Carolina Central University
kind: Public HBCU · Liberal arts & professional (law, business)
affiliation: University of North Carolina System; Thurgood Marshall College Fund
formerNames: National Religious Training School and Chautauqua for the Colored Race
Durham State Normal School for Negroes
description: Founded by pharmacist and Black Wall Street co-founder James E. Shepard (chartered 1909, opened 1910) in Durham's Hayti district, it became in 1925 the nation's first state-funded liberal arts college for Black students. Its law school trained a generation of civil rights lawyers and politicians, and the school sits beside the Parrish Street ‘Black Wall Street’ institutions — North Carolina Mutual and Mechanics & Farmers Bank — whose archives it now holds.

facts.d: Founder James E. Shepard was among the founders of North Carolina Mutual Life Insurance Co. and Mechanics and Farmers Bank.

facts.t: First state-funded Black liberal arts college.
facts.d: Renamed North Carolina College for Negroes in 1925, described as the first state-supported liberal arts college for Black students.
North Carolina Mutual donated its corporate archives to NCCU's James E. Shepard Memorial Library.

sources.label: NCCU Library — NC Mutual Donates Archives

name: Saint Augustine's University
formerNames: Saint Augustine's Normal School and Collegiate Institute
fate: Lost SACSCOC accreditation (final removal July 2025), filed Chapter 11 in April 2026, and cancelled all Fall 2026 classes; not formally closed as of Aug. 2026.
description: Founded in 1867 by Episcopal clergy with first principal Jacob Brinton Smith, it educated Anna Julia Cooper, the Delany family and generations of Black Episcopal clergy and teachers. After years of financial and accreditation crises it filed for bankruptcy in 2026 and suspended instruction, with a bankruptcy judge calling it ‘essentially closed.’

facts.d: Founded under the Episcopal Church's Freedman's Commission; first Black Episcopal bishop Henry B. Delany was an alumnus and administrator.
SACSCOC removed it from membership in July 2025; it filed Chapter 11 in April 2026 and cancelled Fall 2026 classes.

sources.label: JBHE — Saint Augustine's cancels all classes for fall semester (Aug. 2026)
ABC11 — St. Augustine's won't offer classes this fall

name: Shaw University
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society; American Baptist Churches USA; UNCF
description: The oldest HBCU in the South, founded in December 1865 by Rev. Henry Martin Tupper with the American Baptist Home Mission Society. Its Leonard Medical School, pharmacy and law schools trained the doctors, pharmacists and organizers who built Durham's ‘Black Wall Street’ (NC Mutual, Mechanics & Farmers Bank). SNCC was founded on its campus in 1960, and N.C. A&T began as its annex.

facts.d: Shaw/Leonard alumni Aaron M. Moore, W. G. Pearson, S. L. Warren and James E. Shepard were among the founders of North Carolina Mutual and Mechanics & Farmers Bank.
Leonard Medical School (1882–1918) and a law school (1888–1916) operated on campus.
Ella Baker, Shaw class of 1927, convened the April 1960 conference at Shaw that created the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee.

name: Winston-Salem State University
kind: Public HBCU · Teacher education, health sciences
affiliation: University of North Carolina System; Thurgood Marshall College Fund
formerNames: Slater Industrial and State Normal School
description: Founded in 1892 by Simon Green Atkins as Slater Industrial Academy, it became in 1925 the first Black institution in the U.S. authorized to grant degrees for teaching in elementary grades. Under coach Clarence ‘Big House’ Gaines it became a basketball power, producing Earl Monroe and, later, sports-media figure Stephen A. Smith.

facts.d: As Winston-Salem Teachers College (1925) it trained elementary teachers for Black schools across the state.
Its 1967 team, led by Earl ‘The Pearl’ Monroe, won the NCAA College Division title, the first for an HBCU.

name: Central State University
formerNames: Combined Normal and Industrial Department of Wilberforce University
College of Education and Industrial Arts
description: Began in 1887 as a state-funded department on Wilberforce University's campus and separated in 1947, becoming Central State College (1951) and University (1965); Ohio's only public HBCU, it gained 1890 land-grant status in 2014. Graduates include MAXIMA Corp. founder Joshua I. Smith, BET executive Curtis Symonds and opera star Leontyne Price.

facts.d: Created by the Ohio legislature in 1887 as a department of Wilberforce; independent from 1947.
Designated an 1890 land-grant institution in 2014.
Inducts alumni each Charter Day, including Leontyne Price (1948) in 2025.

sources.label: Central State — 138th Charter Day Convocation (Hall of Fame)
Wikipedia — Raymond V. Haysbert (attended Central State & Wilberforce)

connections.label: began as state department of Wilberforce, 1887

name: Payne Theological Seminary
description: The AME Church's seminary, named for Bishop Daniel A. Payne and established on land adjacent to Wilberforce University, carrying on the theological work that dates to Wilberforce's 1856 founding. It is the oldest freestanding African American theological seminary and trains clergy for the AME connection.

facts.d: Honors the AME bishop who bought Wilberforce for the church in 1863.
Appears on the federal-style lists of current HBCUs in Ohio alongside Wilberforce and Central State.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

connections.label: grew out of Wilberforce's theology work

name: Wilberforce University
description: Founded in 1856 by the Methodist Episcopal Church with AME participation and named for abolitionist William Wilberforce; in 1863 the AME Church under Bishop Daniel A. Payne bought it, making it the first college owned and operated by African Americans. Its alumni include Parks Sausage CEO Raymond V. Haysbert, golf-course pioneer Bill Powell, and Lewis College of Business founder Violet T. Lewis.

facts.d: Purchased by the AME Church in 1863 under Bishop Daniel Payne.
A state-funded Combined Normal and Industrial Department, created on its campus in 1887, became Central State University.
Wilberforce's golf team, including future Clearview owner Bill Powell, played Ohio Northern in 1937.
Opened a center for entrepreneurship named for alumni Mark and Shelly Wilson.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Wilberforce opens new center for entrepreneurship

name: Flipper-Key-Davis College
fate: Closed during the Great Depression after the 1935 session (one thesis says 1936).
description: Established by AME Church leaders on the grounds of the former Tullahassee Mission in the all-Black town of Tullahassee (founding dates given variously as 1914–1917), it was Oklahoma's only private Black college until it closed in the Depression.

facts.t: Only private Black college in Oklahoma.
facts.d: It was the only private Black higher-education institution in the state until closing.

sources.label: OU thesis — The Last Hope for African Methodism: Flipper-Key-Davis

name: Langston University
formerNames: Oklahoma Colored Agricultural and Normal University
description: Created in 1897 under the Second Morrill Act in the all-Black town of Langston, it took its current name in 1941 honoring John Mercer Langston. Alumna Ada Lois Sipuel Fisher's Supreme Court victory against the University of Oklahoma law school and Clara Luper's 1958 sit-ins anchor its civil rights legacy; Larzette Hale became the first Black woman with a Ph.D. in accounting and Marques Haynes turned Globetrotter fame into his own touring team.

facts.d: Langston is the sole operating HBCU in Oklahoma.
Larzette Hale (1940) earned a Ph.D. in accounting in 1955, reportedly the first Black woman to do so, and opened a CPA practice in Atlanta.

name: Avery College
affiliation: Methodist Protestant founder; AME, Methodist and Presbyterian ties
fate: Closed in 1873; its three-story building was later demolished for Interstate 279 and a state historical marker (1968) marks the site.
description: Founded in 1849 by Rev. Charles Avery, a Methodist Protestant abolitionist and cotton merchant, as a school and church for African Americans in Allegheny City. It began as an industrial school, added classical studies, and was led 1863–1867 by George Boyer Vashon. Its building reportedly sheltered Underground Railroad freedom seekers.

facts.d: Charles Avery (1784–1858) funded the school with his fortune from cotton and industry.
The basement of its Greek Revival building is reported to have served as an escape route.
AME bishop and publisher Benjamin Tucker Tanner studied at Avery.

name: Cheyney University of Pennsylvania
affiliation: Society of Friends (Quaker founding); Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education
description: Widely cited as the oldest HBCU, it was founded in 1837 with a bequest from Quaker philanthropist Richard Humphreys and became Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth, where Fanny Jackson Coppin built a celebrated classical and industrial program. It moved to a farm in Cheyney in 1902 and is now part of Pennsylvania's state system. Its business alumni include Philadelphia Tribune chief Robert W. Bogle and Rap Snacks founder James Lindsay.

facts.d: Founded in 1837 from Richard Humphreys' Quaker bequest to educate free Black youth.
Under principal Fanny Jackson Coppin the ICY trained teachers and added an industrial department; alumni included Octavius Catto (1858).
Its alumni include Philadelphia Tribune president Robert W. Bogle and Rap Snacks founder James Lindsay (B.S. Marketing).

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of Cheyney University of Pennsylvania alumni

connections.label: founded with Quaker Richard Humphreys' bequest, 1837

name: Lincoln University (Pennsylvania)
description: Chartered in 1854 as the Ashmun Institute by Presbyterian minister John Miller Dickey and his wife Sarah Emlen Cresson, it was renamed for Abraham Lincoln in 1866 and is often called the first degree-granting HBCU. It educated an outsized share of Black professionals and two African heads of state — Kwame Nkrumah and Nnamdi Azikiwe — plus Thurgood Marshall and Langston Hughes. Business alumni include Amsterdam News owner Wilbert Tatum.

facts.d: Chartered by Pennsylvania in 1854 as Ashmun Institute; renamed Lincoln University in 1866.
Lincoln says its graduates made up about 20% of Black physicians and over 10% of Black lawyers in the U.S. between 1854 and 1954.
Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana) and Nnamdi Azikiwe (Nigeria) both graduated from Lincoln.
MacKenzie Scott gave $20 million (2020) and $25 million (2025), the largest gifts in its history.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of Lincoln University (Pennsylvania) alumni

name: Allen University
description: Founded in 1870 in Cokesbury, South Carolina, as Payne Institute by AME ministers including John M. Brown; moved to Columbia and renamed for AME founder Richard Allen in 1880. Alumni include Rev. Clementa C. Pinckney and Briggs v. Elliott organizer Rev. Joseph A. DeLaine.

facts.d: Payne Institute relocated in 1880 and took Richard Allen's name.
The Allen University Historic District was listed on the National Register in 1975.

name: Avery Normal Institute
fate: Closed by the Charleston County school board in 1954 after Brown v. Board; students merged into Burke High School. The Avery Research Center (College of Charleston) now occupies the building.
description: Founded in Charleston in 1865 by the American Missionary Association, Avery trained generations of Black teachers and leaders, among them Septima Clark and NAACP pioneer Edwin Harleston. After it closed, alumni founded the Avery Institute of Afro-American History and Culture, which led to today's Avery Research Center.

facts.d: Avery's normal course prepared Black teachers for South Carolina schools.
The Avery Research Center opened in the building in 1990.

name: Benedict College
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society; American Baptist Churches USA; UNCF
description: Opened in 1870 as Benedict Institute after Bathsheba A. Benedict of Rhode Island, representing the American Baptist Home Mission Society, gave $13,000 for land. Chartered as a college in 1894. Alumni include civil rights leaders Modjeska Monteith Simkins and Septima Clark, funeral-home owner I. S. Leevy Johnson and KFC executive Walt Simon.

facts.d: Bathsheba Benedict's $13,000 bought the land; Rev. Timothy Dodge was the first teacher and president.
Benedict Institute became Benedict College on November 2, 1894.

name: Claflin University
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church (now United Methodist Church); UNCF
description: Founded in 1869 by Methodist Episcopal minister Alonzo Webster to educate freedmen, and named for Massachusetts governor William Claflin and his father Lee Claflin, a Boston philanthropist. South Carolina's oldest HBCU; its alumni include realtor-legislator Earl M. Middleton and photographer Cecil J. Williams.

facts.d: Opened October 27, 1869, as a school for freedmen and their children.
A 2020 gift of $20 million from MacKenzie Scott was the largest single gift in its history.

connections.label: founded by Methodist Episcopal minister Alonzo Webster

name: Clinton College
kind: Private HBCU · AME Zion Christian college
description: Founded in 1894 as Clinton Institute and named for AME Zion Bishop Caleb Isom Clinton of the Palmetto Conference. It became a junior college in 1965 and a four-year college in 2013; it is a very small institution that reported severe cash-flow problems in 2026.

facts.d: Gained accreditation as a four-year institution in 2013 (TRACS).
Reportedly missed employee paychecks and insurance payments in April 2026.

name: Denmark Technical College
formerNames: Denmark Branch of the South Carolina Trade School System
description: Authorized by the South Carolina General Assembly in 1947 and opened in 1948 as a trade school for Black students, teaching tailoring, cosmetology, building trades and auto mechanics. Its motto was "He Who Hath a Trade Hath an Estate." Comedian J. Anthony Brown trained there as a tailor.

facts.d: Opened March 1, 1948, under founding principal Lorry H. Dawkins.
Became Denmark Technical College on gaining SACS accreditation.

name: Friendship College
fate: Closed permanently in 1981 and its buildings were later demolished after a fire.
description: A Baptist school founded in 1891 by Masel Phillip Hall in Rock Hill. Its students formed the Friendship Nine, who in 1961 chose jail over bail after a lunch-counter sit-in, inspiring the "jail, no bail" strategy. NBA champion Harthorne Wingo attended.

facts.d: The 1961 Rock Hill sit-in by Friendship students is commemorated as the Friendship Nine.
The college closed permanently in December 1981.

name: Morris College
affiliation: Baptist Educational and Missionary Convention of South Carolina; UNCF
description: Founded in 1908 by the Baptist Educational and Missionary Convention of South Carolina (organized by Jacob J. Durham), which still owns and operates it. Named for Black community leader Frank Morris; it began as a grade school, high school and college and awarded its first bachelor's degree in 1915.

facts.d: Founded and operated by South Carolina's Black Baptist convention.
Luns C. Richardson led the college from 1974 to 2017.

connections.label: founded by the Baptist Educational and Missionary Convention of SC

name: South Carolina State University
formerNames: Colored Normal Industrial Agricultural and Mechanical College of South Carolina
description: Created by the South Carolina General Assembly in 1896, separating the state's Black land-grant program from Claflin, where it had operated since 1872. SC State is the state's only public 4-year HBCU and the alma mater of Congressman Jim Clyburn and media owner Armstrong Williams. In 1968 it was the site of the Orangeburg massacre.

facts.d: The South Carolina Agricultural and Mechanical Institute began within Claflin College in 1872 before the 1896 act of separation.
On February 8, 1968, state police killed three students and wounded 27 during a protest against a segregated bowling alley.
Hall of Famers Deacon Jones, Harry Carson and Donnie Shell played at SC State.

name: Voorhees University
formerNames: Voorhees Industrial Institute for Colored Youths
description: Founded in 1897 by Tuskegee-trained educator Elizabeth Evelyn Wright as the Denmark Industrial School; New Jersey philanthropist Ralph Voorhees gave $5,000 in 1902 for land and buildings. Affiliated with the Episcopal Church since 1924 and renamed a university in 2022.

facts.d: Elizabeth Evelyn Wright opened the school on April 14, 1897, modeled on Tuskegee.
Became Voorhees University in 2022, its 125th anniversary year.

name: American Baptist College
description: Founded in 1924 as American Baptist Theological Seminary through cooperation between the National Baptist Convention and Southern Baptists, it sits on the old Roger Williams University grounds. Its students—John Lewis, C. T. Vivian, Bernard Lafayette and James Bevel—were central to the Nashville sit-ins and Freedom Rides. It received federal HBCU designation in 2013.

facts.d: Seminarians John Lewis and C. T. Vivian helped lead the 1960 Nashville sit-ins.
Took the name American Baptist College after accreditation by the American Association of Bible Colleges in 1971.

name: Fisk University
affiliation: American Missionary Association; United Church of Christ
description: Founded in 1866 by the American Missionary Association and named for Freedmen's Bureau official Clinton B. Fisk, Fisk is one of the oldest and most storied HBCUs. Its Jubilee Singers toured the world to finance the campus, and its graduates include W. E. B. Du Bois, John Lewis and Nikki Giovanni. Its business line runs through A. Maceo Walker (Universal Life Insurance, Tri-State Bank), builder-CEO Leatrice McKissack and music executive Mathew Knowles.

facts.d: The Fisk Jubilee Singers began touring in 1871 to raise money for the struggling school, funding Jubilee Hall.
Fisk's Carnegie Library (1908) was built by McKissack & McKissack, later led by Fisk alumna Leatrice McKissack.
A. Maceo Walker (B.A. 1930) went from Fisk to NYU and Michigan before running Universal Life Insurance and Tri-State Bank of Memphis.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of Fisk University alumni

connections.label: named for Bureau official Clinton B. Fisk

name: Howe Institute
formerNames: Memphis Baptist Bible and Normal Institute
fate: Struggled in the Great Depression and merged into LeMoyne College in 1937.
description: Founded in Memphis in 1888 by Black Baptists as the Memphis Baptist Bible and Normal Institute, it later became Howe Institute and Howe Junior College. It absorbed Nashville's Roger Williams University around 1929 and was itself absorbed by LeMoyne College in 1937.

facts.d: Roger Williams University (Nashville) combined with Howe in 1929, and Howe merged with LeMoyne in 1937, so both are ancestors of LeMoyne–Owen.

sources.label: Vanderbilt News — Roger Williams University history

name: Knoxville College
affiliation: United Presbyterian Church of North America; Presbyterian Church (USA)
fate: Lost SACS accreditation in 1997 and suspended classes in 2015; approved to reopen in 2018 and operates on a very small scale, seeking accreditation.
description: Founded in 1875 by the United Presbyterian Church of North America (roots in an 1864 mission school), Knoxville College was East Tennessee's leading Black college and absorbed Morristown College in 1989. Accreditation loss in 1997 began a long decline. Alumni include journalist George E. Curry, Chicago Tribune columnist Vernon Jarrett, NIST director Willie E. May and coach Jake Gaither.

facts.d: SACS withdrew accreditation on June 1, 1997; classes were suspended in 2015 with 11 students.
Took over Morristown College as a satellite campus in 1989.

name: Knoxville Medical College
fate: Closed in 1910, hurt by a reputation for weak training and its for-profit model in the Flexner era.
description: A short-lived medical college for Black students in Knoxville's Mechanicsville neighborhood, operating from 1900 to 1910.

facts.d: One of several small Black medical schools that closed around the 1910 Flexner Report.

name: Lane College
description: Founded in 1882 by the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church and led early by Bishop Isaac Lane, Lane College grew from a high school into a four-year college in West Tennessee. Alumni include record promoter Dave Clark, civil rights lawyer Donald Hollowell and St. Louis legislator-developer Leroy Tyus.

facts.d: Established in 1882 as the CME High School; renamed Lane Institute (1883) and Lane College (1896).
Dave Clark (1934) became a pioneering Black record promoter for Decca, Duke/Peacock, Stax and Malaco.

name: LeMoyne College
kind: Private HBCU · Normal school then 4-year college (predecessor)
fate: Merged with Owen College in 1968 to form LeMoyne–Owen College.
description: Begun in 1862 when the AMA sent Lucinda Humphrey to teach freedpeople at Camp Shiloh, the school was destroyed in the 1866 Memphis riot and rebuilt in 1871 with a $20,000 gift from Francis Julius LeMoyne. Its early 'commercial' curriculum trained Memphis Black businesspeople such as grocery-chain founder Bert Roddy, and it absorbed Howe Junior College in 1937.

facts.d: Francis Julius LeMoyne gave $20,000 in 1870 to build the LeMoyne Normal and Commercial School, opened 1871.
Howe Junior College (successor to Roger Williams University) merged into LeMoyne in 1937.

name: LeMoyne–Owen College
affiliation: United Church of Christ; American Missionary Association; Tennessee Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention
formerNames: S. A. Owen Junior College / Owen College
description: LeMoyne–Owen was formed in 1968 by merging LeMoyne College (AMA, roots in an 1862 school for freedpeople at Camp Shiloh) and Owen College (Black Baptist junior college opened 1954). It has been Memphis's Black college through the Memphis sanitation strike era and beyond. Alumni include NAACP leader and savings-and-loan founder Benjamin Hooks, grocery-chain founder Bert Roddy, Tri-State Bank president Jesse H. Turner Sr., and mayors Marion Barry and Willie Herenton.

facts.d: The 1968 merger joined the Congregationalist AMA tradition of LeMoyne with the Black Baptist tradition of Owen College.
LeMoyne students and alumni were linked to Tri-State Bank, Universal Life and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan in Memphis.

connections.label: Owen College side: Tennessee Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention

name: Meharry Medical College
kind: Private HBCU · Medical, dental & graduate school
affiliation: United Methodist Church (founded via Methodist Episcopal Church / Freedmen's Aid Society)
formerNames: Medical Department of Central Tennessee College
description: Meharry opened in 1876 as the medical department of Central Tennessee College (later Walden University), funded in part by the Meharry brothers, and was chartered independently in 1915. It trained a large share of the nation's Black physicians and dentists for a century. Its alumni include Universal Life Insurance founder Dr. J. E. Walker and People's Savings Bank president Dr. Robert F. Boyd, showing how Black doctors became bankers and insurers.

facts.t: First Black medical school in the South.
facts.d: Founded in 1876 as Central Tennessee College's medical department, it was chartered separately as Meharry Medical College in 1915.
Meharry graduates J. E. Walker (Universal Life, Tri-State Bank) and R. F. Boyd (People's Savings Bank and Trust) led Black financial institutions.
Dr. Frank S. Royal (M.D. 1968) sat on the boards of CSX, SunTrust and Smithfield Foods and later chaired Meharry's board.

connections.label: Freedmen's Aid Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church
began as medical department of Central Tennessee College, 1876

name: Morristown College
fate: Financial struggles after desegregation led to its acquisition by Knoxville College in 1989; the campus closed in 1994 (some sources say 1996).
description: Founded in 1881 through the Freedmen's Aid Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church, Morristown trained Black teachers and workers in upper East Tennessee for more than a century. It could not compete with cheaper public colleges after integration and became a Knoxville College satellite before closing. Alumni include comedian Shirley Hemphill and architect DeWitt Dykes Sr.

facts.d: Begun by Almira H. Stearns and organized as a seminary and normal school under the Freedmen's Aid Society.
Wikipedia gives 1994 for the campus closure in its body and 1996 in its lead.

name: Owen College
affiliation: Tennessee Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention
fate: Merged with LeMoyne College in 1968 to form LeMoyne–Owen College.
description: The Tennessee Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention bought property on Vance Avenue in 1947 and opened S. A. Owen Junior College there in 1954. It merged with neighboring LeMoyne College in 1968.

facts.d: Owen was built by the Tennessee Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention, a Black Baptist body.

connections.label: Tennessee Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention

name: Roger Williams University (Nashville)
fate: After two suspicious fires (1905) and financial collapse, the Nashville campus closed and the school combined with Howe Institute in Memphis in 1929.
description: Founded by northern Baptists in 1866 (Bible classes from 1864) as the Nashville Normal and Theological Institute, it became the leading Baptist college for Black Tennesseans. Fires in 1905 forced it off its Hillsboro campus, now part of Vanderbilt's Peabody College; it later merged with Howe Institute, a lineage that runs into LeMoyne–Owen College. Its later campus housed American Baptist College.

facts.d: Its original campus is now part of Vanderbilt University's Peabody College after fires in 1905.
Combined with Howe Institute (1929), which merged into LeMoyne (1937), now LeMoyne–Owen.

name: Swift Memorial College
affiliation: Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. (Board of Missions for Freedmen); Maryville College ties
fate: Closed after desegregation (Wikipedia gives 1952; some sources date the end to 1955).
description: Opened in 1883 by Rev. William Henderson Franklin, the first Black graduate of Maryville College, Swift Memorial served Black students across upper East Tennessee and neighboring states under the Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen. Alumnus William A. Scott II went on to found the Atlanta Daily World and the first chain of Black newspapers.

facts.d: W. H. Franklin led the school from 1883 until 1926.
Wikipedia lists the Scott Newspaper Syndicate founder among its students.

name: Tennessee State University
formerNames: Agricultural and Industrial State Normal School for Negroes
Tennessee Agricultural & Industrial State Normal College
Tennessee Agricultural & Industrial State College (Tennessee A&I)
description: Opened in 1912 as Tennessee's Black land-grant normal school, Tennessee A&I became a powerhouse in athletics (the Tigerbelles under Ed Temple) and teacher training before taking the name Tennessee State University in 1968. Its alumni include Oprah Winfrey, Olympic champion Wilma Rudolph and wireless pioneer Jesse Russell, plus a deep bench of corporate executives and Nashville entrepreneurs.

facts.d: Oprah Winfrey studied communication at TSU on a scholarship while working in Nashville radio and TV, and completed her degree in 1987.
Electrical engineering alumni include Jesse Russell (B.S.E.E. 1972), later an AT&T wireless executive and founder-CEO of incNETWORKS.
The school became Tennessee State University in 1968, and merged with UT-Nashville in 1979 after a desegregation lawsuit.

name: Turner Normal and Industrial School (Turner College)
fate: Moved to Memphis for its last two years and closed in 1932 during the Depression.
description: An AME Church school named for Bishop Henry McNeal Turner, it offered secondary, theological, normal and industrial training in Shelbyville from 1886 before relocating to Memphis and closing in 1932.

facts.d: Established by the AME Church and named for a bishop of the church.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Turner Normal and Industrial School

name: University of West Tennessee College of Medicine and Surgery
affiliation: Independent (founded by Dr. Miles V. Lynk)
fate: One of the Black medical schools that did not survive the post-Flexner Report standards era; closed in 1923.
description: Organized in 1900 by Meharry graduate Dr. Miles V. Lynk and his wife Beebe Steven Lynk (a Lane College graduate), UWT was a Black-founded and Black-run medical college, first in Jackson and from 1907 in Memphis. It is one of the clearest examples of Black physicians building their own educational enterprise.

facts.d: Created by Miles V. Lynk, founder of the Medical and Surgical Observer, the first Black medical journal.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of West Tennessee College of Medicine and Surgery

name: Walden College (Walden University, Nashville)
fate: Closed in 1925 amid financial difficulties and competition from state colleges; its medical department survives as Meharry Medical College.
description: Founded in 1865 by northern Methodist missionaries as Central Tennessee College, renamed Walden University in 1900 for Bishop John M. Walden and Walden College in 1922. Its 1876 medical department became Meharry Medical College, the most consequential Black medical school in the South. Its second campus has housed Trevecca Nazarene University since 1935.

facts.d: The medical department founded in 1876 was chartered separately as Meharry Medical College in 1915.
Alumni include surgeon John Henry Hale and Chattanooga hospital founder Emma Rochelle Wheeler (Meharry, then part of Walden).

name: Bishop College
fate: Lost SACS accreditation in December 1986 under federal debt and falling enrollment, filed Chapter 11 in 1987 and closed in 1988; Paul Quinn College later took over the campus.
description: Founded in Marshall in 1881 by the Baptist Home Mission Society and named for Nathan Bishop, the college moved to South Dallas in 1961 and became a major training ground for Black Baptist preachers. Alumni include publishing-and-banking pioneer R. H. Boyd, insurance and funeral magnate Mack H. Hannah Jr., novelist-publisher Sutton E. Griggs and Dallas pastor Frederick Haynes III.

facts.d: Relocated from Marshall to a new South Dallas campus.
SACS revoked accreditation in Dec. 1986, cutting off federal programs and UNCF funds; bankruptcy failed and the college closed in 1988.
R. H. Boyd built the National Baptist Publishing Board and a Nashville bank; Mack H. Hannah Jr. became perhaps the wealthiest Black Texan of his era.

connections.label: campus taken over by Paul Quinn, 1990

name: Butler College
fate: Closed in summer 1972 after enrollment fell to 58 students in 1968; it never achieved four-year accreditation.
description: Founded in 1905 by the East Texas Baptist Association as Texas Baptist Academy, the coeducational school was renamed Butler College in 1924 for its president C. M. Butler. The Texas Baptist Convention helped operate it from 1932.

facts.d: Became Butler College in 1924, honoring C. M. Butler.
Fell to 58 students by 1968; closed 1972.

connections.label: founded by East Texas Baptist Association

name: Conroe College
kind: Private HBCU · Normal & industrial / Bible college
affiliation: American Baptist Convention of Texas (Black Baptist)
fate: Declined through financial mismanagement and competition and closed in 2011; the site was sold in 2014 and preservationists are working to save the building.
description: Opened in April 1903 by Dr. Jimmie Johnson and his wife Chaney, who sold their own farm to fund a school for African Americans less than 40 years after the Civil War. Its religious program was funded by the Houston-based American Baptist Convention of Texas.

facts.d: The Johnsons funded the school with proceeds from their farm.
A nonprofit is working to restore the deteriorating building.

sources.label: Houston Landing — Nonprofit works to restore historic Conroe College

connections.label: supported by American Baptist Convention of Texas

name: Guadalupe College
formerNames: College of the Guadalupe Baptist Association
fate: Reverted to junior-college status in 1931; a fire destroyed its main building on February 9, 1936 and efforts to restore it failed.
description: Founded in 1884 by the Guadalupe Baptist Association of Black congregations, it was the only Black Baptist institution of higher learning in South Texas. Philanthropist George W. Brackenridge funded buildings and land, and enrollment peaked above 450 in 1907.

facts.d: The only Black Baptist institution of higher learning in South Texas.
The main building burned in 1936.

name: Huston–Tillotson University
affiliation: United Methodist Church; United Church of Christ
description: Austin's oldest institution of higher learning, Huston–Tillotson was formed on October 24, 1952 by the merger of Tillotson College (an American Missionary Association school) and Samuel Huston College (a Methodist Episcopal school). It became a university in 2005. Its alumni include U.S. Treasurer Azie Taylor Morton.

facts.d: Tillotson College and Samuel Huston College merged to form Huston–Tillotson College; it became Huston–Tillotson University on February 28, 2005.
Before joining the Kansas City Monarchs, Jackie Robinson served as athletic director at Samuel Huston College and coached its 1944–45 basketball team.
Azie Taylor Morton (B.S. 1956) became the only African American to serve as Treasurer of the United States.

name: Jarvis Christian University
description: Planned by the Negro Disciples of Christ of Texas, the school was built on 456 acres donated by Major James Jones Jarvis and Ida Van Zandt Jarvis to the Christian Women's Board of Missions, on condition it remain a school for Black students. Instruction began in 1913. It is the only surviving HBCU of the twelve founded by the Disciples of Christ.

facts.d: The Jarvises donated 456 acres to the Christian Women's Board of Missions.

facts.t: Last of the Disciples' Black colleges.
facts.d: Only HBCU remaining of the twelve founded by the Disciples of Christ.
Renamed from Jarvis Christian College and added graduate programs in 2023.

name: Mary Allen College
kind: Private HBCU · Women's seminary / junior college
affiliation: Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen; later General Missionary Baptist Convention of Texas
fate: Closed in 1943 when Presbyterian funding ended, revived in 1944 under Black Baptist ownership, and finally closed after operating as a junior college until 1977.
description: Rooted in Rev. Samuel Fisher Tenney's 1871 Crockett Presbyterian Sabbath School, Mary Allen opened in 1886 as a seminary for Black women, named for Mary Esther Allen of the Board of Missions for Freedmen's Women's Executive Committee. It educated thousands of Black women and later men for nearly nine decades.

facts.d: Mary Esther Allen chaired the Women's Executive Committee of the Board of Missions for Freedmen from 1884.
After a 1943 closure, the General Missionary Baptist Convention of Texas owned and ran it from 1944.

sources.label: Amistad Research Center — Mary Allen College records

connections.label: operated by Texas Black Baptist convention from 1944

name: Paul Quinn College
formerNames: Connectional School for the Education of Negro Youth
description: Founded in Austin in 1872 by AME preachers, the school moved to Waco in 1877 and was chartered as Paul Quinn College in 1881. In 1990 it moved to Dallas onto the former Bishop College campus, acquired from businessman Comer Cottrell. Under president Michael Sorrell it became the nation's first urban work college and turned its football field into the WE over ME Farm with PepsiCo.

facts.t: Early HBCU west of the Mississippi.
facts.d: AME preachers founded it in Austin on April 4, 1872; it is described as the first HBCU established west of the Mississippi River.
Relocated to southeast Dallas in 1990 on the former Bishop College grounds.
Sorrell ended football in 2007; the WE over ME Farm, created with PepsiCo, was dedicated in 2010.
SACS moved against its accreditation in 2009; the college joined TRACS in 2011.

sources.label: Handbook of Texas — Bishop College (Paul Quinn occupies campus)

name: Prairie View A&M University
affiliation: State of Texas (Texas A&M University System); 1890 land-grant
formerNames: Alta Vista Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas for Colored Youth
Prairie View State Normal & Industrial College
Prairie View A&M College of Texas
description: Authorized by the Texas Legislature in 1876 as the Black branch of the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas, Prairie View opened in 1878 as Alta Vista Agricultural College with eight students. It became Texas' second-oldest public university and a pipeline of Black teachers, engineers and military officers. Its MBA program produced oil executive Kase Lawal, and its engineering school produced founder-engineers such as Freweini Mebrahtu.

facts.d: Authorized in 1876 under the Morrill Act framework; eight students enrolled at Alta Vista Agricultural College in March 1878.

facts.t: Renamed Prairie View A&M University in 1973.
facts.d: Earlier names include Prairie View State Normal & Industrial College and Prairie View A&M College of Texas.
Retired Lt. Gen. Julius Becton (1989–1994) and former Brown University president Ruth Simmons (2017–2023) both led the school.

sources.label: Handbook of Texas — Prairie View A&M University

name: Samuel Huston College
fate: Merged with Tillotson College in 1952 to form Huston–Tillotson College.
description: Samuel Huston College grew out of an 1876 Methodist Episcopal conference and was developed under an 1883 agreement with the Freedmen's Aid Society; it was named for Iowa donor Samuel Huston. Jackie Robinson worked there as athletic director and basketball coach in 1944–45 before his professional baseball career.

facts.d: Named for Samuel Huston of Marengo, Iowa.
Robinson took the athletic director job at the invitation of college president Rev. Karl Downs.

connections.label: founded via Methodist Episcopal conference / Freedmen's Aid Society

name: Southwestern Christian College
description: Founded in Fort Worth in 1948 as Southern Bible Institute by educator-minister G. P. Bowser, the school moved to Terrell in 1949 onto the former Texas Military College campus. Jack Evans Sr., its first Black president, led it for fifty years (1967–2017).

facts.d: Moved to Terrell in fall 1949 after buying the closed Texas Military College campus.
Jack Evans Sr. served 1967–2017.
SACS accreditation to award associate and bachelor's degrees.

name: St. Philip's College
affiliation: Founded by Episcopal Diocese of West Texas; now Alamo Colleges District
formerNames: St. Philip's Normal and Industrial School
description: Founded March 1, 1898 by Episcopal Bishop James Steptoe Johnston as a weekend sewing class for six Black girls, St. Philip's grew under Artemisia Bowden — administrator for 52 years — into a high school and junior college. It joined San Antonio's public junior college system in 1942 and is the westernmost HBCU in the United States.

facts.d: Began with missionary Alice G. Cowan teaching six girls.
Daughter of a formerly enslaved man, she led the school from 1902 for 52 years.
Public historically Black community college on San Antonio's East Side.

connections.label: founded by Episcopal Bishop of West Texas

name: Texas College
description: Founded January 9, 1894 in Tyler by ministers of the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church to serve Black students excluded from Texas' segregated universities. Briefly called Phillips University (1909–1912). Alumna Mildred Fay Jefferson became the first Black woman to graduate from Harvard Medical School.

facts.d: Established by a group of CME ministers in 1894.
Named for Bishop Henry Phillips 1909–1912 before becoming Texas College.
The D.R. Glass Library (1948) is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Texas Southern University
description: Begun in 1927 as Houston Colored Junior College holding evening classes at Jack Yates High School, the school became Houston College for Negroes and was taken over by the state in 1947 as Texas State University for Negroes — a response to Heman Sweatt's lawsuit against the University of Texas law school. It is home to the Thurgood Marshall School of Law and the Jesse H. Jones School of Business, and its alumni include Barbara Jordan, Mickey Leland, oil executive Kase Lawal and investment manager Gerald B. Smith.

facts.d: In 1947, amid Sweatt v. Painter, the Texas Legislature passed Senate Bill 140 creating Texas State University for Negroes and took over Houston College for Negroes as its base.
Hugh Roy Cullen donated the current campus site.
The Jesse H. Jones School of Business hosts the Gerald B. Smith Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation, endowed by alumnus Gerald B. Smith.

sources.label: Texas Southern University — Jesse H. Jones School of Business alumni

name: Tillotson College
fate: Merged with Samuel Huston College in 1952 to form Huston–Tillotson College.
description: Chartered in 1877 by the American Missionary Association and named for Congregational minister George Jeffrey Tillotson, the school opened on January 17, 1881. It operated as a women's college from 1926 to 1935 before merging with Samuel Huston College in 1952.

facts.d: Tillotson Collegiate and Normal Institute opened January 17, 1881 after its 1877 charter.
It was a women's college from 1926 to 1935.

name: Wiley University
description: Founded in 1873 in Marshall by the Freedmen's Aid Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church and credited to Bishop Isaac Wiley, it is one of the oldest Black colleges west of the Mississippi. Melvin B. Tolson's debate teams — dramatized in The Great Debaters — beat national champion USC in 1935. Alumni include CORE co-founder James Farmer, Heman Sweatt, Opal Lee, and early Black bank founder H. Claude Hudson.

facts.d: Tolson's teams lost only 1 of 75 debates over 15 years; Denzel Washington gave $1 million in 2007 to restore the program.
Known as Wiley College from 1929 to 2023, it returned to the Wiley University name with new graduate programs.
Alumnus Lee Wilder Thomas struck oil in the 1920 Mexia boom and later co-built Simmons Royalty Co. in Oklahoma.

connections.label: founded by Freedmen's Aid Society of the M.E. Church

name: Bishop Payne Divinity School
fate: Closed in 1949; its work for Black Episcopal clergy was absorbed by the (historically white) Virginia Theological Seminary in Alexandria.
description: An Episcopal school in Petersburg that trained Black clergy for the church in the South; it began as a normal and industrial school and did not award bachelor's degrees until 1910. Saint Paul's College founder James Solomon Russell studied here from 1878.

facts.d: Founded 1878 in Petersburg.
Admitted in 1878; went on to found Saint Paul's College.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Hampton University
description: Founded in 1868 by the American Missionary Association under former Union general Samuel Chapman Armstrong, on ground where Mary S. Peake had taught freedpeople beneath the Emancipation Oak since 1861. Hampton's industrial-education model trained Booker T. Washington and shaped Tuskegee and dozens of other schools. Its alumni run deep in Black business history — from Chicago Defender founder Robert S. Abbott to Oracle president Charles Phillips (MBA) and Baltimore Ravens president Sashi Brown.

facts.d: The university dates its origins to September 17, 1861, when Mary S. Peake began teaching freedmen for the American Missionary Association.
Hampton held Virginia's land-grant program for Black students until 1920, when it moved to Virginia State.
The Hampton University Museum is described as the oldest African diaspora museum in the United States.
Robert S. Abbott (1896) and his nephew John H. Sengstacke (1934) — the two men who built and ran the Chicago Defender — both studied at Hampton.

sources.label: Hampton University School of Business — Notable Alumni

name: Hartshorn Memorial College
fate: Merged into Virginia Union University in 1932, making VUU coeducational.
description: Founded in Richmond in 1883 as a college for African American women under Baptist sponsorship. For nearly half a century it educated Black women teachers and missionaries before merging into neighboring Virginia Union.

facts.d: Established specifically for African American women.
Its merger made Virginia Union coeducational.

name: Norfolk State University
formerNames: Norfolk Unit (Division) of Virginia Union University
description: Opened September 18, 1935, as the Norfolk Unit of Virginia Union University with about 85 students, it became independent in 1942, was folded into Virginia State College in 1944, and separated again in 1969. Today it is Virginia's largest HBCU by many measures, with a School of Business whose entrepreneurship institute bears the name of auto-dealer alumnus Ernest M. Hodge.

facts.t: Born as a Virginia Union branch.
facts.d: Founded in 1935 as the Norfolk Unit of Virginia Union University; renamed Norfolk Polytechnic College in 1942.
Separated from Virginia State and gained SACS accreditation in 1969; university status in 1979.
The Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship honors the 1975 business graduate who built one of the largest Black-owned auto dealership groups.
Received $40 million (2020) and $50 million (2025) gifts.

sources.label: NSU — Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship

connections.label: began as Norfolk Unit of VUU, 1935

name: Richmond Theological Seminary
fate: Merged with Wayland Seminary in 1899 to form Virginia Union University.
description: The Richmond branch of the ABHMS's National Theological Institute, holding classes by November 1865 and from 1867 meeting in Lumpkin's Jail under Nathaniel Colver. Incorporated as Richmond Institute in 1876 and re-established as Richmond Theological Seminary in 1886, it trained early Black Baptist leaders such as businessman-educator James H. Blackwell (1880).

facts.d: Nathaniel Colver resumed the school in 1867 in the former slave-trading jail.
Joined Wayland Seminary to create Virginia Union University.

name: Saint Paul's College
formerNames: Saint Paul Normal and Industrial School
fate: Lost SACS accreditation over finances and faculty credentials; after a planned merger with Saint Augustine's fell through in May 2013, it closed June 30, 2013.
description: Founded in 1888 by Hampton-trained Episcopal priest James Solomon Russell, who had begun teaching in a church room in 1883, as Saint Paul Normal and Industrial School. At its peak about 1,000 students attended; by closing it had about 150, and the campus was later sold.

facts.d: James Solomon Russell bought the first building with a legacy from the Rev. Saul of Philadelphia.
SACS revoked accreditation; a court injunction briefly reinstated probation before trustees chose to close.
The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation sold most of the campus in 2017 for $2.5 million.

sources.label: Episcopal News Service — St. Paul's College to close (2013)
Diverse Issues in Higher Education — After 125 years, St. Paul's shutting down
Lost Colleges — St. Paul Normal and Industrial School

name: Virginia State University
description: Chartered by the Virginia legislature on March 6, 1882, as the Virginia Normal and Collegiate Institute, it is described as the first fully state-supported four-year institution of higher learning for Black Americans; John Mercer Langston was its first president. It became Virginia's 1890 land-grant HBCU when the program moved from Hampton in 1920. Its business school is named for alumnus Reginald F. Lewis, the TLC Beatrice financier.

facts.d: Opened October 1, 1883 after a lawsuit delayed it 19 months; 126 students and seven faculty in year one.
The federal land-grant program for Black Virginians moved from Hampton Institute to the school in 1920.

facts.t: Reginald F. Lewis College of Business.
facts.d: The business college carries the name of its 1965 alumnus, described by the school as 'America's First Black Billionaire Businessman'.
Received $30 million in 2020 and $50 million in 2025 — the largest single gift in its history.

sources.label: VSU Reginald F. Lewis College of Business — Alumni

name: Virginia Union University
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society; American Baptist Churches USA
description: Founded in 1865 by the American Baptist Home Mission Society to train freedmen for ministry, it met for a time in the former Lumpkin's Jail slave pen. Virginia Union formed in 1899 when Richmond Theological Seminary merged with Washington's Wayland Seminary; Hartshorn Memorial College joined in 1932 and Storer College's endowment in 1964. It produced Governor L. Douglas Wilder, Pittsburgh Courier publisher Robert L. Vann, and the Richmond bankers who ran Consolidated Bank and Trust.

facts.d: From 1867 the school was housed in the building long known as Lumpkin's Jail.
Richmond Theological Seminary and Wayland Seminary merged to form Virginia Union University; first classes met October 4, 1899.
Hartshorn Memorial College merged in 1932 (making VUU coeducational) and Storer College merged its assets in 1964.
Norfolk State began in 1935 as VUU's Norfolk Unit.

name: Virginia University of Lynchburg
description: Organized in May 1886 at the 19th annual session of the Virginia Baptist State Convention, it was founded and run by Black Baptists rather than a white missionary society — an early model of Black institutional self-reliance. Civil-rights forerunner Vernon Johns graduated in 1915 and later served as its president.

facts.d: Organized by the Black Virginia Baptist State Convention in 1886.
The 1915 graduate served as president 1929–1933 before leading Montgomery's Dexter Avenue Baptist Church.

connections.label: founded by Virginia Baptist State Convention, 1886

name: University of the Virgin Islands
affiliation: Government of the U.S. Virgin Islands; land-grant
description: Founded in 1962 as the College of the Virgin Islands and designated an HBCU in 1986, when it took its current name. UVI has educated much of the Caribbean's political leadership, including USVI Governor Albert Bryan Jr. (MBA) and Sint Maarten Prime Minister Silveria Jacobs.

facts.d: The only HBCU outside the continental U.S.; designated in 1986.
Alumni include heads of government and ministers across the Eastern Caribbean.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of the Virgin Islands

name: Bluefield State University
description: Founded February 28, 1895, as the Bluefield Colored Institute under principal Hamilton Hatter (a Storer College graduate) to serve the Black families of the southern West Virginia coalfields. After desegregation it became majority white; a 1968 bombing of the gym led the president to close the dorms, accelerating that shift. It returned to residential life in 2021 and became a university in 2022.

facts.d: Opened with 40 pupils in 1895, became a normal school in 1909 and a teachers college in 1932.
A bomb damaged the gym on November 21, 1968; dorms were closed and the student body became predominantly white.
Became residential again in 2021 for the first time since 1968; renamed a university in 2022.

name: Storer College
affiliation: Free Will Baptists; Freedmen's Bureau support
fate: Closed in June 1955 after West Virginia withdrew state funding following Brown v. Board — the last blow after decades without tuition revenue, accreditation or a meaningful endowment; its campus is now part of Harpers Ferry National Historical Park.
description: Grew from a one-room school for freedpeople opened in 1865 by Free Will Baptist missionary Nathan Cook Brackett, with a $10,000 matching gift from Maine philanthropist John Storer; it was chartered in 1867–68 on former Armory property. It hosted the Niagara Movement's 1906 conference, the first in the U.S. Alumni included Nigeria's Nnamdi Azikiwe, jazz arranger Don Redman and lawyer-publisher J. R. Clifford.

facts.d: Hosted the movement's second conference in 1906, led by W. E. B. Du Bois — a forerunner of the NAACP.
Began four-year degrees in 1938 but never won regional accreditation.
Its endowment and library went to Virginia Union University; the campus became part of the national park.

sources.label: NPS — Dr. Madison Spencer Briscoe, Storer College and Harpers Ferry NHP

name: West Virginia State University
description: Established under the Second Morrill Act in 1891 as the West Virginia Colored Institute, it added college degrees in 1915 and in 1927 became the first public college in the state accredited by the North Central Association. Historian Carter G. Woodson served as academic dean. It lost land-grant status in 1957 and regained it fully in 2001; it is now majority white.

facts.d: State funding for land-grant matching ended in 1957; Congress fully restored the status in 2001 after a 12-year effort.
In 1939 it was the first of six HBCUs authorized to offer an aviation program; graduates flew with the Tuskegee Airmen.
NASA mathematician Katherine Johnson, NBA pioneer Earl Lloyd, Judge Damon Keith and OIC founder Leon Sullivan.

name: AME Zion Church
description: African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church (1821). It sponsors Livingstone College and Clinton College and founded Lomax-Hannon.

name: African Methodist Episcopal Church
description: The first independent Black denomination in the U.S. (1816). It founded Wilberforce, Allen, Morris Brown, Paul Quinn, Edward Waters and Shorter, among others, entirely with Black-raised money.

name: American Baptist Home Mission Society
description: Northern Baptist society that founded Morehouse, Spelman, Shaw, Virginia Union, Benedict, Bishop and Florida Memorial's predecessors.

name: American Missionary Association
description: Protestant abolitionist society (1846) that founded or co-founded more Black colleges after the Civil War than any other body, including Fisk, Hampton, Talladega, Tougaloo, Dillard's predecessor Straight, LeMoyne and Tillotson.

name: Black Baptist conventions
description: The National Baptist Convention and state Black Baptist conventions, which founded and ran colleges such as Selma University, Arkansas Baptist, Simmons College of Kentucky and Morris College.

name: Catholic Church / Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament
description: St. Katharine Drexel's Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament founded Xavier University of Louisiana (1915/1925), the only Catholic HBCU.

name: Christian Church (Disciples of Christ)
description: Sponsors Jarvis Christian University in Texas.

name: Christian Methodist Episcopal Church
description: Founded in 1870 as the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church. Its schools include Lane, Miles, Paine (with the Methodists) and Texas College.

name: Churches of Christ
description: Sponsors Southwestern Christian College in Terrell, Texas.

name: Episcopal Church / American Church Institute
description: Through the American Church Institute for Negroes (1906), the Episcopal Church supported Saint Augustine's, Saint Paul's and Voorhees.

name: Freedmen's Bureau
description: Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands (1865–1872). It funded buildings, land and teachers for many early Black colleges, and Howard University is named for its commissioner, Gen. Oliver O. Howard.

name: Julius Rosenwald Fund
description: The Sears, Roebuck president's fund (1917–1948) built Rosenwald schools across the South and funded Black colleges, fellowships and Dillard University.

name: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod
description: Through the Synodical Conference's Black mission, the Lutherans ran Immanuel Lutheran College (Greensboro) and Alabama Lutheran Academy, later Concordia College Alabama.

name: Methodist Episcopal Church / Freedmen's Aid Society
description: Northern Methodists' Freedmen's Aid Society (1866) and its United Methodist successor founded or supported Clark, Claflin, Rust, Wiley, Bennett, Philander Smith, Dillard's predecessor New Orleans University, Bethune-Cookman, Huston-Tillotson and Meharry.

name: Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen
description: Northern Presbyterian mission board behind Johnson C. Smith, Barber-Scotia, Knoxville College, Stillman (Southern Presbyterian), Mary Holmes and Swift Memorial.

name: Religious Society of Friends (Quakers)
description: Quaker philanthropist Richard Humphreys's 1837 bequest founded the Institute for Colored Youth, now Cheyney University, the oldest HBCU.

name: Second Morrill Act (1890)
description: Required states that segregated their land-grant colleges to fund a Black land-grant institution. It created or designated the 19 "1890 land-grant" HBCUs, including NC A&T, FAMU, Prairie View, Alcorn and Tennessee State.

name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
description: Founded Oakwood University in Huntsville, Alabama (1896).

name: Thurgood Marshall College Fund
description: Founded in 1987 to support the public HBCUs and predominantly Black institutions with scholarships, capacity building and corporate partnerships.

name: UNCF (United Negro College Fund)
description: Founded in 1944 by Tuskegee president Frederick D. Patterson so private HBCUs could raise money together. Its member colleges form the largest network on this map.

name: United Church of Christ
description: Successor to the Congregational churches behind the American Missionary Association. Historically affiliated with Fisk, Dillard, Huston-Tillotson, Talladega, Tougaloo and LeMoyne-Owen.

name: A. Maceo Walker
hbcuStory: Earned a bachelor's in business administration at Fisk University (1930), then an MBA from NYU (1932) and a master's in actuarial science from Michigan (1935)—reportedly the only Black actuary in Tennessee at the time.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Indianola, Mississippi, in 1909; sold Universal Life policies during summers as a student.
breakthrough: Joined Universal Life's audit department, its board in 1935 and became president in 1952; co-founded Tri-State Bank of Memphis with his father in 1946 and became its president in 1958.
legacy: Expanded Universal Life into multiple states and kept Tri-State a going concern; handed Universal to his daughter Patricia Walker-Shaw in 1983 and returned after her death until 1990.

breakthroughDetail.d: Trained as an actuary before running the family insurer.
President of Universal Life (from 1952) and Tri-State Bank (from 1958).

legacyDetail.d: Tri-State's boardroom hosted sit-in planning and it kept its vault open at night for protesters' bail (per Jesse Turner Jr.).

name: A. Philip Randolph
hbcuStory: Graduated as valedictorian of Cookman Institute's 1907 class in Jacksonville.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Crescent City, Florida, son of an AME minister.
breakthrough: Co-founded The Messenger magazine (1917) and from 1925 led the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, winning a Pullman contract in 1937.
legacy: Led the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

breakthroughDetail.d: First major Black-led union contract, 1937.

legacyDetail.d: Chaired the 1963 march.

name: Aaron McDuffie Moore
hbcuStory: Entered Shaw University in 1885 and finished Leonard Medical School's four-year program in three years, passing the N.C. medical boards in 1888 (second of 46). Later a Shaw trustee.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Columbus County, N.C.; trained first at normal schools in Lumberton and Fayetteville.
breakthrough: Durham's first Black physician co-founded North Carolina Mutual and Provident Association with John Merrick in 1898, serving as treasurer/medical director and, from 1919, president.
legacy: Founded Durham Drug Co. (1895), Lincoln Hospital (1901) and its nursing school, and the library that became the Stanford L. Warren branch; used Rosenwald matching grants to improve rural Black schools.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded the company with John Merrick; became president after Merrick's death in 1919.
Founded Durham's Black hospital in 1901 and a nursing school in 1903.

legacyDetail.d: His drugstore, hospital, library and insurer anchored Durham's Black Wall Street.
Daughter Lyda married Edward R. Merrick, joining the two founding families.

sources.label: Wikipedia — North Carolina Mutual Life Insurance Company

connections.label: attended the Normal School at Fayetteville

name: Aaron Shirley
hbcuStory: Graduated from Tougaloo College in 1955 before Meharry Medical College.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in rural Mississippi.
breakthrough: Became the first Black pediatric resident at the University of Mississippi Medical Center and pioneered community health centers.
legacy: Founded the Jackson Medical Mall, converting a dying shopping mall into a health and business hub; MacArthur Fellow.

breakthroughDetail.d: Redeveloped a failing mall into a medical campus.

legacyDetail.d: Recognized for community health work.

name: Ada Lois Sipuel Fisher
hbcuStory: Graduated from Langston University in 1945.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Chickasha, Oklahoma, in 1924.
breakthrough: Won Sipuel v. Board of Regents (1948) against the University of Oklahoma law school and later graduated from it.
legacy: Returned to Langston as a professor and administrator.

breakthroughDetail.d: Supreme Court victory in 1948.

legacyDetail.d: Later taught at Langston.

name: Al Attles
hbcuStory: Graduated from N.C. A&T in 1960 after starring in basketball.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Newark, N.J.
breakthrough: Spent his entire career with the Warriors as player, NBA-champion head coach (1975) and later general manager and vice president.
legacy: Naismith Hall of Famer (2019) and one of the NBA's first Black coaches.

breakthroughDetail.d: Coached Golden State to the championship.

legacyDetail.d: Over 60 years with the franchise.

name: Al Bell
hbcuStory: Wikipedia's Philander Smith alumni table lists Al Bell (born Alvertis Isbell) among the college's notable graduates, in his hometown of Little Rock.
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1940 and raised in Arkansas, he started as a disc jockey in Little Rock.
breakthrough: Joined Stax Records in 1965 as promotions director and in 1969 became co-owner—the first African American with equity in the label—rebuilding its catalog after the Atlantic split with hits such as Isaac Hayes's Hot Buttered Soul.
legacy: Made Stax the second-largest Black-owned business of the 1970s, later served as president of Motown Records Group during its sale, and founded Bellmark Records, which released Tag Team's 'Whoomp! (There It Is).'

breakthroughDetail.d: Became co-owner of Stax in 1969 when co-founder Estelle Axton sold her shares.
His promotion of the 'Memphis sound' made Stax the second-largest African-American–owned business in the 1970s (per Wikipedia).
President of Motown Records Group during its restructuring; then launched his own label, Bellmark.

legacyDetail.d: The BBC called him 'the driving force behind Stax Records' in 2009.

name: Albert Bryan Jr.
hbcuStory: Earned an MBA from the University of the Virgin Islands in 2003 (B.A. economics, Wittenberg, 1989).
humbleBeginnings: Born on St. Thomas.
breakthrough: Served as Virgin Islands labor commissioner (2007–2015) and chair of the Economic Development Authority board, then ran consulting firms Aabra Group and Master Strategies.
legacy: Elected the 9th governor of the U.S. Virgin Islands in 2018 and re-elected in 2022.

breakthroughDetail.d: In office since January 7, 2019.

legacyDetail.d: One of several Caribbean heads of government educated at UVI.

name: Albert W. Dent
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morehouse in 1926 with an accounting degree, working at Atlanta Life Insurance Company while a student.
humbleBeginnings: Worked at Atlanta Life Insurance while still a student.
breakthrough: After serving as a branch office auditor for Atlanta Life, he became business administrator of New Orleans' Black-owned Flint-Goodridge Hospital and then president of Dillard University (1941–1969).
legacy: Built Dillard and Flint-Goodridge into pillars of Black New Orleans health care and education.

breakthroughDetail.d: Took a job as branch office auditor for Atlanta Life after graduating.
Led Dillard University for 28 years.

legacyDetail.d: Expanded hospital care for poor Black patients in New Orleans.

name: Alex Haley
hbcuStory: Attended Alcorn A&M briefly before Elizabeth City State Teachers College, then left to join the Coast Guard.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Henning, Tennessee, by his grandmother's family of storytellers.
breakthrough: Co-wrote The Autobiography of Malcolm X and wrote Roots (1976), adapted into the landmark 1977 miniseries.
legacy: Pulitzer special citation 1977.

breakthroughDetail.d: Book and ABC miniseries phenomenon.

legacyDetail.d: Special citation, 1977.

name: Alexander B. Cummings Jr.
hbcuStory: After a B.S. in finance and economics at Northern Illinois University, earned an MBA in finance from Clark Atlanta University (as reported).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Monrovia; studied at Cuttington University College before leaving for the U.S.
breakthrough: Joined Pillsbury in 1982, becoming VP of finance for its international businesses, then spent 20 years at Coca-Cola, retiring in 2016 as chief administrative officer.
legacy: Returned to Liberia to lead the Alternative National Congress and chairs the Cummings Africa Foundation.

breakthroughDetail.d: Retired as chief administrative officer in 2016.
VP of finance for Pillsbury's international businesses.

legacyDetail.d: Chairs the Cummings Africa Foundation; Liberian presidential candidate.

sources.label: Coca-Cola — Alexander B. Cummings to retire

connections.label: MBA in finance (reported as Clark Atlanta)

name: Alexis Herman
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in sociology from Xavier University of Louisiana in 1969.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Mobile, Alabama.
breakthrough: Became the first African-American U.S. Secretary of Labor (1997–2001) after directing the White House Office of Public Liaison.
legacy: After government she chaired and ran New Ventures, Inc., and sat on the boards of Coca-Cola, Cummins, MGM Resorts and Entergy.

breakthroughDetail.d: Joined the board in 2002.

legacyDetail.d: Chair and CEO of New Ventures, Inc.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Labor — Hall of Secretaries: Alexis Herman
Xavier University — community mourns Alexis Herman

name: Alfred C. Liggins III
hbcuStory: Took night classes at the University of the District of Columbia while working at WOL, without graduating; later earned a Wharton MBA (1995). He grew up in D.C. after his mother took a job at Howard and funded the 2016 renaming of Howard's Cathy Hughes School of Communications.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Omaha to Cathy Hughes; moved to D.C. at seven, graduated from Woodrow Wilson High School in 1983 and briefly worked as a sales executive at Light Records in California while attending night classes at UCLA.
breakthrough: Worked at the family's WOL while studying, then became president and CEO of Radio One in 1997, taking it public in 1999 and building out TV One (2004, with Comcast) and 21 stations bought from Clear Channel.
legacy: Runs Urban One — about 56 radio stations in 16 markets plus TV One — and expanded it into casino gaming; with his mother he endowed Howard's communications school.

breakthroughDetail.d: Became president and CEO of Radio One in 1997 while his mother remained owner and chair.
Launched TV One in 2004 in partnership with Comcast; it reached 59 million households by 2020.

legacyDetail.d: His multimillion-dollar 2016 gift through the family foundation renamed Howard's School of Communications for Cathy Hughes.

sources.label: MetroMBA — Urban One CEO Alfred Liggins

connections.label: 2016 gift renaming the Cathy Hughes School of Communications

name: Alice Coachman
hbcuStory: Recruited to Tuskegee Institute's track program in 1939, she won national titles there before finishing a degree at Albany State College (1949).
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Albany, Georgia, training barefoot on dirt roads in the segregated South.
breakthrough: Won high-jump gold at the 1948 London Olympics — the first Black woman to win Olympic gold.
legacy: Became the first Black female athlete to land a major corporate endorsement (Coca-Cola, 1952).

breakthroughDetail.d: First Black woman Olympic champion.
A first for a Black female athlete.

legacyDetail.d: Started a foundation for young athletes.

name: Alice Walker
hbcuStory: Enrolled at Spelman in 1961 on a state scholarship; mentored by Howard Zinn and Staughton Lynd, she transferred to Sarah Lawrence after Zinn's firing (graduated 1965).
humbleBeginnings: Born to sharecroppers in Eatonton, Georgia; injured in a childhood accident.
breakthrough: Her novel The Color Purple (1982) made her the first African American woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.
legacy: The novel became a film, a Broadway musical and a second film.

breakthroughDetail.d: For The Color Purple.

name: Althea Gibson
hbcuStory: Graduated from Florida A&M in 1953, where she attended on an athletic scholarship.
