humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Harlem, learning the game in street paddle tennis.
breakthrough: Became the first Black player to win a Grand Slam title (1956 French Championships) and won Wimbledon and the U.S. title in 1957 and 1958.
legacy: Won 11 Grand Slam titles and later became the first Black woman on the LPGA tour.

breakthroughDetail.d: 11 titles in singles and doubles.

legacyDetail.d: Broke tennis's color line in the 1950s.

name: Amanda America Dickson
hbcuStory: Left her father's plantation at 27 to attend the normal school of Atlanta University (1876–1878), studying teaching.
humbleBeginnings: Born into slavery as the daughter of white planter David Dickson and Julia Frances Lewis, a girl he enslaved.
breakthrough: Inherited her father's estate — including about 17,000 acres in Hancock and Washington counties — in 1885 after the will survived a court challenge by white relatives.
legacy: Became one of the wealthiest African American women of the 19th century; her Augusta home has been restored as a landmark.

breakthroughDetail.d: The estate she inherited in 1885.
Her inheritance was upheld by the Georgia Supreme Court.

legacyDetail.d: Held major property in post-Reconstruction Georgia.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Amanda America Dickson
Augusta Chronicle — Restoration highlights Augusta's first African American millionaire

name: Amanda Gray Hilyer
hbcuStory: Attended Howard after moving to D.C. around 1897 and earned her pharmacy degree in 1903; later left bequests to Howard.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Atchison, Kansas; married pharmacist Arthur S. Gray in 1893.
breakthrough: Opened the Fountain Pharmacy at 12th and U Streets NW with her husband in 1905, becoming the first Black woman to own and operate a pharmacy in Washington.
legacy: A civic leader in Black Washington who supported the NAACP, the Phillis Wheatley YWCA and Howard.

breakthroughDetail.d: First Black woman to own and operate a pharmacy in Washington.
Located in the heart of the U Street Black business district.

legacyDetail.d: Left gifts to Howard University and community institutions.

sources.label: Library of Congress — Inside Adams: A family of pharmacists

name: Amiri Baraka
hbcuStory: Transferred from Rutgers to Howard in 1952 and left without a degree.
humbleBeginnings: Born Everett LeRoi Jones in Newark.
breakthrough: His 1964 play 'Dutchman' won an Obie; he founded the Black Arts Movement's Black Arts Repertory Theatre/School.
legacy: Poet laureate of New Jersey; father of Newark mayor Ras Baraka, also a Howard graduate.

breakthroughDetail.d: Obie Award-winning 1964 play.
A founding figure.

legacyDetail.d: Son Ras Baraka became mayor of Newark.

sources.label: New York Times — Baraka's Dutchman staged in a bathhouse

name: Amy Sherald
hbcuStory: Began at Clark Atlanta on a pre-med track, cross-registered for painting at Spelman under Arturo Lindsay, and graduated with a B.A. in painting (1997).
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Columbus, Georgia.
breakthrough: Painted Michelle Obama's official portrait for the National Portrait Gallery (2018).
legacy: Her paintings now command major auction prices and museum retrospectives.

breakthroughDetail.d: Unveiled in 2018.

sources.label: The New Yorker — The Amy Sherald effect

name: Andrew Young
hbcuStory: Attended Dillard University for a year before graduating from Howard (B.S. 1951).
humbleBeginnings: Born in New Orleans to a dentist and a teacher.
breakthrough: A top aide to Martin Luther King Jr. in the SCLC, he became a Georgia congressman, U.N. ambassador and two-term mayor of Atlanta.
legacy: Helped win the 1996 Olympics for Atlanta and co-founded the consulting firm GoodWorks International.

breakthroughDetail.d: Served under President Carter (1977–79).
Led Atlanta 1982–90.

legacyDetail.d: Championed international investment in Atlanta.

sources.label: Biographical Directory of the U.S. Congress — Andrew Young

name: André Leon Talley
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in French literature from North Carolina Central University in 1970, then an M.A. at Brown.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Washington, D.C., and raised by his grandmother, a domestic worker at Duke, in Durham.
breakthrough: From an unpaid apprenticeship with Diana Vreeland, he moved through Interview and WWD to Vogue, where he became the magazine's first African American male creative director (1988–95) and later editor-at-large.
legacy: A cultural power broker who pushed for runway diversity and mentored designers and models; Chevalier of the French Ordre des Arts et des Lettres (2020).

breakthroughDetail.d: Fashion news director 1983–87, creative director 1988–95, editor-at-large 1998–2013.

legacyDetail.d: Mentored figures including Naomi Campbell and LaQuan Smith.

sources.label: Wikipedia — North Carolina Central University (notable alumni)

name: Andy Shallal
wealthNote: Estimated from ownership of a multi-unit restaurant chain; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Enrolled in Howard University's medical school after graduating from Catholic University; later earned an MBA from Maryland's Smith School.
humbleBeginnings: Moved to the U.S. from Iraq in 1966 with his family; his father was the Arab League's ambassador. He worked as a medical immunology researcher at NIH.
breakthrough: Opened Busboys and Poets at 14th and V Streets NW in September 2005, a restaurant-bookstore-performance venue whose name comes from the works of Langston Hughes.
legacy: Expanded Busboys and Poets across the D.C. region, ran for D.C. mayor in 2014, and founded several peace and voting-rights organizations.

breakthroughDetail.d: Opened the flagship on U Street corridor; grew to multiple D.C.-area locations.
Candidate in the 2014 D.C. mayoral election.

legacyDetail.d: Received DCVote's Champions of Democracy Award in 2010.

sources.label: Washington Post — Andy Shallal is running for D.C. mayor

name: Ann Walton Kroenke
wealthNote: Forbes figure cited by Wikipedia; Black Enterprise reported more than $4B earlier.
hbcuStory: Graduated from Lincoln University in Jefferson City with a nursing degree, according to Black Enterprise, which called her the HBCU world's wealthiest graduate. Wikipedia also lists Lincoln University as her alma mater.
humbleBeginnings: Daughter of James 'Bud' Walton, Sam Walton's brother and early partner in Walmart; she trained as a nurse.
breakthrough: Inherited a large block of Walmart stock from her father after his death in 1995, making her a billionaire.
legacy: Is the principal owner of the NBA's Denver Nuggets (2016–) and NHL's Colorado Avalanche (2015–), part of Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, and is married to Stan Kroenke.

breakthroughDetail.d: She and her sister Nancy Walton Laurie inherited Walmart stock from Bud Walton.
Principal owner of the Denver Nuggets and Colorado Avalanche.

legacyDetail.d: Black Enterprise identifies her as the wealthiest HBCU graduate, reportedly worth more than $4 billion.

connections.label: owner of Denver Nuggets & Colorado Avalanche

name: Anna Julia Cooper
hbcuStory: Began at Saint Augustine's Normal School in Raleigh at age nine (on scholarship) and later taught there before Oberlin.
humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in Raleigh, N.C.
breakthrough: Wrote A Voice from the South (1892), led Washington's M Street (Dunbar) High School, and at 66 earned a doctorate from the Sorbonne.
legacy: Quoted in U.S. passports; a founding voice of Black feminist thought.

breakthroughDetail.d: Landmark 1892 work of Black feminism.

legacyDetail.d: Fourth African American woman to earn a doctorate.

name: Anne Moody
hbcuStory: Attended Natchez Junior College on a basketball scholarship, then earned a B.S. from Tougaloo College in 1964.
humbleBeginnings: Born to sharecroppers near Centreville, Mississippi.
breakthrough: Joined the 1963 Jackson Woolworth's sit-in and wrote the memoir Coming of Age in Mississippi (1968).
legacy: Her memoir remains a core civil-rights text.

breakthroughDetail.d: Jackson, 1963.

legacyDetail.d: Published 1968.

name: Ardie Clark Halyard
hbcuStory: Graduated from Atlanta University with a degree in education.
humbleBeginnings: Moved north in the Great Migration; worked for Goodwill Industries for 20 years while keeping the books for her own institution.
breakthrough: In 1925 she and her husband Wilbur co-founded Columbia Savings and Loan Association, Milwaukee's first Black-owned savings and loan, opening with a single ten-dollar bill and drawing no salary for a decade.
legacy: Columbia's assets reached about $4 million by the late 1960s; she was the first woman president of Milwaukee's NAACP.

breakthroughDetail.d: Columbia Savings and Loan opened with one ten-dollar bill.
By the late 1960s.

legacyDetail.d: Let Black Milwaukeeans borrow without racial discrimination.

sources.label: Women in Wisconsin — Ardie Clark Halyard

name: Arian Simone
hbcuStory: Earned her bachelor's and MBA at Florida A&M (entering class of 1999); inducted onto the SBI Big Board in 2024 and endowed an SBI scholarship.
humbleBeginnings: Has described experiencing homelessness while building her first businesses before turning to venture investing.
breakthrough: Co-founded the Fearless Fund with fellow FAMU alumna Ayana Parsons, a VC fund for women-of-color founders backed by PayPal, Bank of America and Costco.
legacy: The FAMU Foundation invested in the fund in 2021, its first investment in a Black-led VC firm; the fund drew a high-profile 2023 legal challenge to its grant program.

breakthroughDetail.d: Pre-seed to Series A investor in women-of-color-led companies.
Backers include PayPal, Bank of America, Invest Atlanta and Costco.

legacyDetail.d: FAMU Foundation became an LP in 2021.
Endowed the Arian Simone Fearless Fund scholarship at SBI.

sources.label: WCTV — FAMU Foundation invests in Fearless Fund
Entrepreneur — She was homeless; now she runs a $25 million investment fund

name: Armstrong Williams
wealthNote: Estimate only: no published figure; based on ownership of multiple TV station licenses and their sales.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in political science and English from South Carolina State in 1981.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Marion, South Carolina.
breakthrough: Co-founded the Graham Williams Group marketing and PR firm in 1991 and founded Howard Stirk Holdings in 2013 to buy television stations alongside Sinclair Broadcast Group.
legacy: By 2015 he was the largest African American owner of U.S. TV stations; HSH has owned stations including WEYI (Flint), WXBU (Harrisburg) and WWMB (Myrtle Beach).

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded April 2013; named for his parents.
Held that distinction in 2015 until Byron Allen passed him in 2019.

legacyDetail.d: Bought and later sold several stations through HSH.

sources.label: Wikipedia — South Carolina State University (notable alumni)

name: Art Shell
hbcuStory: Graduated from Maryland State College (now UMES) in 1968.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in North Charleston, South Carolina.
breakthrough: Hall of Fame offensive tackle for the Raiders; in 1989 became the NFL's first Black head coach of the modern era.
legacy: Pro Football Hall of Fame (1989).

breakthroughDetail.d: Named Los Angeles Raiders head coach in 1989.

legacyDetail.d: Inducted 1989.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of Maryland Eastern Shore (notable alumni)

name: Arthenia J. Bates Millican
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in English from Morris College in 1941 and chaired its English department 1947–49.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Sumter, South Carolina.
breakthrough: Published Seeds Beneath the Snow (1969) and The Deity Nodded (1973) while teaching at Southern University.
legacy: Earned an LSU Ph.D. (1972) and an NEA fellowship (1976).

breakthroughDetail.d: Short stories, poetry and novels.

name: Arthur R. Collins
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in accounting from Florida A&M in 1982 (honorary doctorate 2009); in 2001 he became the first chairman of FAMU's Board of Trustees. Inaugural SBI Hall of Fame inductee.
humbleBeginnings: Began his career as an IBM systems engineer in 1982 and later served as deputy receiver at the Florida Department of Insurance.
breakthrough: Founded Public Private Partnership, Inc., a Tallahassee strategic-planning and political consulting firm, in 1989.
legacy: Co-founded theGROUP in Washington in 2011 and has served on the boards of RLJ Lodging Trust and the Brookings Institution; he chairs Morehouse School of Medicine's board.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded 1989 and led as president and CEO.
Founding and managing partner of the D.C. strategy, policy and communications firm (2011).
Senior political strategist to Barack Obama's 2008 campaign.

legacyDetail.d: RLJ Lodging Trust, Brookings Institution, Meridian International Center.

name: Arthur Shores
hbcuStory: Graduated from Talladega College.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Wenonah (Birmingham), Alabama; taught school while studying law by correspondence.
breakthrough: Alabama's leading Black civil-rights attorney, representing Autherine Lucy and others; his home was repeatedly bombed.
legacy: Became Birmingham's first Black city councilman (1968).

breakthroughDetail.d: Represented Autherine Lucy in her UA desegregation case.

legacyDetail.d: Appointed 1968.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Alabama — Arthur Davis Shores

connections.label: her attorney in the UA case

name: Asa T. Spaulding
hbcuStory: After graduating from Durham's National Training School (now NCCU) in 1923, he took business classes at Howard, then earned an accounting degree magna cum laude at NYU and a master's in actuarial science at Michigan (1932).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Columbus County, N.C.; grand-nephew of N.C. Mutual co-founder Dr. Aaron McDuffie Moore and cousin of C.C. Spaulding, he clerked at the company as a youth.
breakthrough: Became North Carolina Mutual's actuary in 1932 — widely called America's first Black actuary — joined its board in 1938 and served as president from 1958/59 to 1968.
legacy: Under his presidency N.C. Mutual dedicated its 1966 Durham headquarters, the city's tallest building for 19 years; he was a leader of the National Negro Insurance Association.

breakthroughDetail.d: Trained at Michigan and applied actuarial analysis to the nation's largest Black business.
Led the company for roughly a decade until 1968.

legacyDetail.d: The 1966 N.C. Mutual tower was Durham's tallest building for 19 years.

sources.label: American Academy of Actuaries — Remembering a titan of actuarial acumen
Durham County Library — Asa T. Spaulding Biographical Collection

name: Autherine Lucy
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in English from Miles College in 1952.
humbleBeginnings: Youngest of ten children of a farming family in Shiloh, Alabama.
breakthrough: In 1956 became the first Black student admitted to the University of Alabama, before being expelled amid riots.
legacy: The University later named a building for her; she earned a UA master's in 1992.

breakthroughDetail.d: Enrolled 1956.

legacyDetail.d: UA's Autherine Lucy Hall named in 2022.

name: Autumn Adeigbo
hbcuStory: Graduated from Spelman with a degree in economics, then from Parsons School of Design in fashion design (2005).
humbleBeginnings: Of Nigerian heritage.
breakthrough: Founded her eponymous women's ready-to-wear and accessories brand, dressing clients including Amanda Gorman and Kerry Washington.
legacy: Became the first Black female designer–led brand to raise more than $1 million in venture capital.

breakthroughDetail.d: First brand led by a Black female designer to raise over $1 million in VC.

legacyDetail.d: Brand built on women-made, globally sourced production.

sources.label: Los Angeles Times — She dresses Amanda Gorman

name: Azie Taylor Morton
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in commercial education from Huston–Tillotson College in 1956.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Dale, Texas; rejected by the University of Texas graduate school because of her race.
breakthrough: Served as Treasurer of the United States (1977–1981) under President Carter — the only African American to hold the post — with her signature on U.S. currency.
legacy: Her signature on the nation's money made her a symbol for Black women in finance.

breakthroughDetail.d: September 1977–January 1981.

legacyDetail.d: Her name appeared on U.S. paper money.

name: Barbara Gardner Proctor
hbcuStory: Graduated from Talladega College in three years with a degree in English and education, adding psychology and sociology in 1954.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Black Mountain, North Carolina; worked in teaching, counseling and social work before entering the music business.
breakthrough: After writing liner notes at Vee-Jay Records — where she arranged the label's 1963 Beatles deal with EMI — and winning awards at Post-Keyes-Gardner, she founded Proctor & Gardner Advertising in 1970 with a U.S. Small Business Administration loan — the first ad agency owned by a Black woman.
legacy: Her agency quickly became the second-largest Black-owned ad agency in the U.S.; it filed for bankruptcy in 1995, and she remained a Chicago civic figure and WTTW trustee.

breakthroughDetail.d: First advertising agency founded by a Black woman.
Brought the Beatles' first U.S. releases via a 1963 EMI deal.
Became second-largest Black-owned agency soon after founding.

legacyDetail.d: Showed SBA-backed capital could launch a Black-owned creative firm.

sources.label: New York Times — Barbara Gardner Proctor obituary

name: Barbara Jordan
hbcuStory: Graduated magna cum laude from Texas Southern University in 1956, where she starred on the debate team, before Boston University law school.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Houston's Fifth Ward, daughter of a Baptist minister.
breakthrough: First African American elected to the Texas Senate since Reconstruction (1966) and first Southern Black woman elected to Congress (1972); her 1974 Watergate impeachment speech made her a national figure.
legacy: Chaired the U.S. Commission on Immigration Reform until her death and taught at UT's LBJ School.

breakthroughDetail.d: Served 1967–1973; acting governor for a day in 1972.
Represented Texas' 18th District 1973–1979.

legacyDetail.d: Fellow TSU alumnus Mickey Leland succeeded her in the 18th District.

name: Barrington Irving
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in aeronautical science, magna cum laude, from Florida Memorial University.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Kingston, Jamaica; raised in Miami.
breakthrough: In 2007 became the youngest person and first Black pilot to fly solo around the world, in a plane named Inspiration.
legacy: Founded the nonprofit Experience Aviation (2005) and the Flying Classroom STEM curriculum (2013).

breakthroughDetail.d: 24,600 miles, March–June 2007.

legacyDetail.d: Based at Opa-Locka Executive Airport.

name: Barry Hankerson
hbcuStory: Attended Central State University in Ohio, majoring in sociology and playing on the football team.
humbleBeginnings: Born in New York City and raised in Harlem; worked as a community organizer in Detroit Mayor Coleman Young's office in the early 1970s.
breakthrough: Managed The Winans, Toni Braxton and R. Kelly, and in 1993 formed Blackground (later Blackground Records) to launch his niece Aaliyah's career via a Jive distribution deal.
legacy: Also founded publisher Black Fountain Music and Blackground Pictures; his control of the Blackground catalog has been the subject of long-running disputes with Aaliyah's estate and artists.

breakthroughDetail.d: Released Aaliyah's debut Age Ain't Nothing but a Number through Jive.
The Winans, Toni Braxton, R. Kelly.

legacyDetail.d: Re-released the Blackground catalog in 2021 amid estate objections.

name: Barry Mayo
hbcuStory: Graduated from Howard, where he was the first general manager of the student station WHBC.
humbleBeginnings: Attended Brooklyn Technical High School.
breakthrough: Helped launch WRKS in New York in 1981 — the first station to play rap — and became RKO General's first Black general manager.
legacy: First Black GM of Emmis Radio New York (WRKS, Hot 97), then president of radio at Radio One (2007).

breakthroughDetail.d: Helped launch WRKS in 1981.
Named president of radio at Radio One in 2007.

legacyDetail.d: WHBC to Radio One illustrates Howard's communications-to-ownership pipeline.

sources.label: Vassar Musical Urbanism — How the sound of New York came from four Brooklyn high schools

name: Bayard Rustin
hbcuStory: Attended Cheyney (then a state teachers college) in the 1930s.
humbleBeginnings: Raised by Quaker-influenced grandparents in West Chester, Pennsylvania.
breakthrough: Chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington.
legacy: Awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously (2013).

breakthroughDetail.d: Organized the 1963 march.

legacyDetail.d: Adviser to Martin Luther King Jr.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of Cheyney University of Pennsylvania alumni

name: Ben Ali
wealthNote: Estimated from ownership of a single landmark restaurant business; no published figure.
hbcuStory: After attending four universities he earned his bachelor's degree from Howard; he came to the U.S. in 1945 intending to become a doctor.
humbleBeginnings: Born in San Juan, Trinidad, the eldest of seven in a Muslim Indo-Caribbean family descended from indentured laborers; arrived in the U.S. as a student in 1945.
breakthrough: With his wife Virginia he opened Ben's Chili Bowl on U Street in 1958, building it into a Black Washington institution.
legacy: Ben's became a destination for presidents and celebrities and remains family-run by Virginia and their sons, with additional locations.

breakthroughDetail.d: Ben's Chili Bowl opened on U Street NW in 1958.
The restaurant has attracted presidents, celebrities and politicians for decades.

legacyDetail.d: Virginia Ali and their sons continued the business after Ben's death in 2009.

sources.label: New York Times Magazine — Ben Ali

name: Ben Ruffin
hbcuStory: Graduated from North Carolina Central University in 1964 (political science), then earned an MSW at UNC-Chapel Hill.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Durham and educated at Hillside High; led anti-poverty and housing efforts in Durham in the 1960s.
breakthrough: After serving as Gov. Jim Hunt's special assistant for minority affairs and a vice president at North Carolina Mutual, he joined RJR Nabisco in 1986 and became vice president for corporate affairs at R.J. Reynolds Tobacco in 1989, steering minority-supplier and hiring initiatives.
legacy: In 1998 became the first Black chair of the UNC Board of Governors; later ran his own Winston-Salem consultancy, The Ruffin Group.

breakthroughDetail.d: VP for Corporate Affairs at R.J. Reynolds Tobacco from 1989.
Vice president and special assistant to the president of North Carolina Mutual for two years.

legacyDetail.d: Chaired the UNC Board of Governors from 1998.

sources.label: Wikipedia — North Carolina Central University (notable alumni)

name: Benjamin Hooks
hbcuStory: Studied pre-law at LeMoyne College (1941–43) before Howard and DePaul law school (J.D. 1948).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Memphis in 1925; served in the Army in Italy.
breakthrough: Co-founded Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association in Memphis in 1955 and later chaired it; became the first Black FCC commissioner (1972).
legacy: Led the NAACP from 1977 to 1993; Presidential Medal of Freedom 2007.

breakthroughDetail.d: Mutual Federal Savings and Loan, 1955.

legacyDetail.d: Executive director, 1977–1993.

name: Benjamin Tucker Tanner
hbcuStory: Studied at Avery College in Allegheny City (Pittsburgh).
humbleBeginnings: Born free in Pittsburgh.
breakthrough: Edited the AME Church's Christian Recorder and founded the A.M.E. Church Review.
legacy: Elected an AME bishop; father of painter Henry Ossawa Tanner.

breakthroughDetail.d: Long-time editor of the Christian Recorder.

legacyDetail.d: Elected 1888.

name: Bennett M. Stewart
hbcuStory: Earned his bachelor's degree from Miles College in 1936.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Huntsville, Alabama.
breakthrough: Spent seventeen years with Atlanta Life Insurance Co., becoming its Illinois director and opening its Chicago branch in 1951.
legacy: Parlayed his insurance network into Chicago politics, serving in Congress 1979–81.

breakthroughDetail.d: Led the company's Chicago expansion.

legacyDetail.d: Illinois 1st district, 1979–81.

sources.label: Biographical Directory of the U.S. Congress — Stewart

name: Bennie Thompson
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. from Tougaloo College (1968) and an M.S. from Jackson State (1972).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Bolton, Mississippi.
breakthrough: Mayor of Bolton, Hinds County supervisor, then U.S. Representative since 1993.
legacy: Chaired the House Homeland Security Committee and the January 6 committee.

breakthroughDetail.d: Mississippi's 2nd district.

legacyDetail.d: Homeland Security; January 6 select committee.

sources.label: Biographical Directory of the U.S. Congress — Thompson

name: Bernard Kinsey
hbcuStory: Graduated from Florida A&M in 1967, where he met his wife Shirley (FAMU English, 1967); later earned a Pepperdine MBA and received an honorary doctorate from FAMU.
humbleBeginnings: Born in West Palm Beach; after FAMU he was hired as the first Black sales representative at Humble Oil.
breakthrough: Spent about two decades at Xerox, becoming a vice president, then co-chaired and served as COO of Rebuild L.A. after the 1992 uprising.
legacy: With Shirley he built the Kinsey Collection, one of the largest private collections of African American art and history, which has toured nationally.

breakthroughDetail.d: Rose to vice president during a roughly 20-year Xerox career.
Co-chairman and COO of Rebuild L.A. under Peter Ueberroth, recruiting private investment after the 1992 unrest.

legacyDetail.d: Family-owned collection spanning 1632 to the present, now run by son Khalil.
Returned as a 2025 FAMU commencement speaker.

name: Bernice King
hbcuStory: Graduated from Spelman (class of 1985) before earning M.Div. and J.D. degrees at Emory.
humbleBeginnings: Youngest child of Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King; five years old when her father was assassinated.
breakthrough: Became CEO of the King Center for Nonviolent Social Change in 2012.
legacy: Leads the King family's institutional legacy in Atlanta.

breakthroughDetail.d: Has led the King Center since 2012.

name: Bert M. Roddy
hbcuStory: Attended LeMoyne Normal School after his family moved to Memphis (Wikipedia lists him as class of 1910).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Augusta, Arkansas, in 1886 to Jerry and Harriette McKenny Roddy.
breakthrough: Founded a chain of grocery stores, becoming the first African American to own a grocery chain in Memphis.
legacy: Co-founded a restaurant and theater and the Coloured Citizens Association, and organized and served as first president of the Memphis NAACP branch.

breakthroughDetail.t: First Black grocery chain in Memphis.
breakthroughDetail.d: Wikipedia credits him as the first Black owner of a grocery store chain in Memphis.
Also organized a theater and co-founded a restaurant.

legacyDetail.d: First president of the Memphis NAACP chapter; active in the Lincoln League.

name: Bess Freedman
hbcuStory: Earned her J.D. from the University of the District of Columbia's law school after an Ithaca College undergraduate degree.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Troy, New York; practiced as an assistant state's attorney and a Legal Aid Society attorney.
breakthrough: Moved into real estate at the Corcoran Group in 2003, joined Brown Harris Stevens in 2013 and became its first CEO in 2018.
legacy: Leads the New York luxury brokerage and has publicly criticized real estate's 'good ole boys club' culture.

breakthroughDetail.d: First CEO of Brown Harris Stevens (2018).
Senior managing director of Corcoran's East Side headquarters.

legacyDetail.d: Profiled by Forbes on gender barriers in real estate.

sources.label: Forbes — New Brown Harris Stevens CEO says good ole boys club alive and well

name: Beverly Harvard
hbcuStory: Graduated from Morris Brown College with a B.A. in sociology at 22.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Macon, Georgia, graduating from Ballard-Hudson High School.
breakthrough: Rose through the Atlanta Police Department and became chief in 1994 — the first Black woman to lead a major U.S. city's police force.
legacy: Oversaw policing for the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.

breakthroughDetail.d: First Black woman police chief of a major U.S. city.

name: Bill Winston
hbcuStory: Graduated from Tuskegee Institute in 1967, then flew fighters in Vietnam (Distinguished Flying Cross).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Tuskegee, Alabama; served six years in the Air Force before joining IBM as a marketer in 1973.
breakthrough: Rose to IBM regional marketing manager, left in 1985 for ministry, and founded Living Word Christian Center (1988–90), which bought the 33-acre Forest Park Mall in Illinois.
legacy: Built a church-anchored business ecosystem — the Joseph Business School, Forest Park Plaza, bookstores, an aviation company and Washington Plaza in Tuskegee.

breakthroughDetail.d: Living Word acquired the 33-acre Forest Park Mall; first service there New Year's Eve 1997.
Founded an accredited campus and online business school in Forest Park.

legacyDetail.d: Lists Washington Plaza in Tuskegee among his ventures.

name: Bob Hayes
hbcuStory: Ran track and played football at Florida A&M.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Jacksonville, Florida.
breakthrough: Won the 100 meters at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and became a Dallas Cowboys star receiver.
legacy: The only athlete with both an Olympic gold medal and a Super Bowl ring; inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2009.

breakthroughDetail.d: Olympic 100m champion, 1964.

legacyDetail.d: Pro Football Hall of Fame 2009.

name: Bonita C. Stewart
wealthNote: Estimated from senior tech-executive compensation; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in journalism from Howard, then an MBA from Harvard Business School.
humbleBeginnings: Began in corporate marketing at IBM and DaimlerChrysler and co-founded Nia Enterprises, an online publishing and marketing company, and a formal-wear rental business.
breakthrough: Joined Google in 2006 and in 2011 became the first Black woman named a Google vice president; as VP of Global Partnerships she managed the largest U.S. publisher relationships.
legacy: Serves as a board partner at Gradient Ventures and advisor to CapitalG, and co-wrote 'A Blessing: Women of Color Teaming Up to Lead, Empower and Thrive.'

breakthroughDetail.d: Named vice president at Google in 2011.
Her team oversaw the largest U.S. publishers across search, mobile apps, commerce and news.

legacyDetail.d: Board partner at Gradient Ventures and advisor to CapitalG, Google-linked venture arms.

sources.label: Crain's New York — Most Powerful Women 2019: Bonita Stewart

name: Bonner Upshaw III
hbcuStory: Starred at power forward for Alcorn State basketball (1984–87); Alcorn invited him back as commencement speaker in 2020.
humbleBeginnings: Played ten seasons of pro basketball in France, Portugal, Macedonia and Switzerland, working at a Detroit-area PEO in the off-seasons.
breakthrough: In 2012 he and partner David L. Stone merged their PEO firms to form Trion Solutions, which he leads as CEO.
legacy: Trion grew to more than 500 client companies and 45,000+ worksite employees, billed as the largest minority-owned PEO in the U.S.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded via merger with David L. Stone.
500+ clients, 45,000+ worksite employees (2020).

legacyDetail.d: 2020 commencement speaker.

sources.label: Alcorn State — Trion Solutions CEO Bonner Upshaw III commencement speaker
HBCU Connect — Upshaw named Alcorn grad speaker

name: Booker T. Washington
hbcuStory: Walked much of the 500 miles to Hampton Institute, worked as a janitor to pay his way and graduated in 1875 under Samuel Chapman Armstrong; also studied at Wayland Seminary (1878–79).
humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in Virginia; worked in West Virginia salt furnaces and coal mines as a boy.
breakthrough: Became the first principal of Tuskegee Institute in 1881 and, in 1900, founded the National Negro Business League.
legacy: Built Tuskegee into a national institution and networked Black entrepreneurs through the NNBL; Hampton remains the model he spread across the South.

breakthroughDetail.d: First leader of Tuskegee Institute.
Organized Black business owners nationally.

legacyDetail.d: Exported Hampton's industrial-education philosophy.

name: Brad Holmes
hbcuStory: Graduated cum laude from N.C. A&T in 2002 with a B.S. in journalism and mass communication; a four-year letterman who captained the 1999 MEAC and Black college national champions.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Tampa, Fla.; played defensive tackle at A&T.
breakthrough: Rose from a 2003 Rams public-relations internship through scouting to director of college scouting, then was named executive vice president and general manager of the Detroit Lions in 2021.
legacy: Rebuilt the Lions into a contender; named PFWA Executive of the Year in 2023 and 2024.

breakthroughDetail.d: Hired Jan. 2021; first move was the Stafford-for-Goff trade.
PFWA honors in 2023 and 2024.

legacyDetail.d: One of few HBCU graduates running an NFL front office.

name: Buck Buchanan
hbcuStory: Attended Grambling (1959–1962) on a scholarship from Eddie Robinson, earning Academic All-American honors.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Gainesville, Alabama, raised in Birmingham.
breakthrough: First overall pick of the 1963 AFL draft and Hall of Fame defensive tackle for the Kansas City Chiefs.
legacy: After football he ran construction and advertising businesses and a restaurant, and served as president of Kansas City's Black Chamber of Commerce (1986–1989).

breakthroughDetail.d: Inducted 1990.
Construction, advertising and restaurant ventures.

sources.label: Pro Football Hall of Fame — Buck Buchanan
Alabama Sports Hall of Fame — Buck Buchanan

name: Buck O'Neil
hbcuStory: Finished high school and took two years of college courses at Edward Waters College in Jacksonville.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Sarasota, Florida, which had no high school for Black students.
breakthrough: Kansas City Monarchs star and manager; became MLB's first Black coach with the Cubs in 1962.
legacy: Elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2022 and awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom (2006).

breakthroughDetail.d: Chicago Cubs, 1962.

legacyDetail.d: Inducted 2022.

connections.label: attended (high school & two years of college)

name: Calvin E. Booker Sr.
hbcuStory: Played football for UAPB (1975–79) and earned a bachelor's in education in 1979; he later coached and worked in UAPB's education dean's office, alumni office and recruiting, and became national president of the UAPB/AM&N Alumni Association.
humbleBeginnings: Became the youngest person elected to the Pine Bluff City Council in the late 1980s.
breakthrough: Joined Waste Management in Dallas in 1991 and rose to corporate vice president of public affairs for its Southern Group in Atlanta, covering 12 Southeastern states and Puerto Rico.
legacy: Chaired the Corporate Round Table of the National Black Caucus of State Legislators for four years; named National Alumni President of the Year by the National Black College Alumni Association.

breakthroughDetail.d: Corporate vice president of public affairs, Southern Group.

legacyDetail.d: President of the UAPB/AM&N National Alumni Association.

sources.label: Pine Bluff Commercial — UAPB grad named national alumni president
Pine Bluff Commercial — UAPB alumni president to speak at convocation

name: Calvin E. Tyler Jr.
wealthNote: Estimated: the couple's $25 million in documented gifts implies wealth above that level from UPS compensation and stock.
hbcuStory: Entered Morgan State College in 1961 to study business administration but left in 1963 when he could not pay tuition; he and wife Tina later gave Morgan $5 million (2016) and $20 million (2021).
humbleBeginnings: Took a job in 1964 as one of UPS's first ten drivers in Baltimore after leaving Morgan for lack of money.
breakthrough: Climbed from the delivery truck to senior vice president of operations at UPS, retiring in 1998.
legacy: The Calvin and Tina Tyler Endowed Scholarship Fund — believed to be the largest alumni gift to any HBCU at the time — now funds students nationwide.

breakthroughDetail.d: Rose from one of the first UPS drivers in Baltimore to senior vice president of operations.
Built wealth through a 34-year UPS career (employee-ownership culture).

legacyDetail.d: Largest private gift from an alumnus in Morgan State history, announced 2021.
Their 2016 gift for Baltimore City students was then the largest in Morgan's history.

sources.label: Morgan State — Former UPS Driver Gives Morgan $20 Million
Baltimore Sun — Morgan State alumnus gives $20 million
ABC News — College dropout donates $20 million

name: Calvin Rolark
hbcuStory: Earned a bachelor's degree in business administration from Prairie View College (now Prairie View A&M); he also attended Tennessee State, Michigan State and Cornell.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Texarkana, Texas, he worked as an editor of the Memphis World in the 1940s before moving to Washington.
breakthrough: Founded The Washington Informer newspaper in 1962, giving D.C.'s Black community its own weekly voice.
legacy: Founded the United Black Fund in 1969 as a Black-led alternative to United Way; the Informer remains in his family's hands.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded 1962.
Founded 1969 to fund Black and Latino community organizations.

legacyDetail.d: The Informer continued under his family after his 1994 death.

sources.label: Washington Post — Crusading publisher Calvin Rolark dies (1994)

name: Calvin Smyre
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in business administration from Fort Valley State University.
humbleBeginnings: From Columbus, Georgia.
breakthrough: Elected to the Georgia House in 1974 and became its longest-serving member, while working as executive vice president of corporate external affairs at Columbus-based Synovus and president of the Synovus Foundation.
legacy: Nominated U.S. ambassador to the Bahamas in 2022.

breakthroughDetail.d: Executive VP of corporate external affairs at Synovus.

sources.label: Georgia General Assembly — Calvin Smyre bio

name: Carl J. Murphy
hbcuStory: Graduated from Howard in 1911, then earned a Harvard master's (1913) and a doctorate at Jena; he taught German and chaired Howard's German department (1913–18), where he met his wife Vashti Turley.
humbleBeginnings: Son of John H. Murphy Sr., who founded and ran the Baltimore Afro-American.
breakthrough: Joined the Afro in 1918 and took over after his father's death in 1922, expanding it into a chain with editions in Washington, Philadelphia, Newark and Richmond.
legacy: Led the paper for over 40 years, served on the NAACP board from 1931 and as president of the National Newspaper Publishers Association (1954–55).

breakthroughDetail.d: Expanded the Afro-American into regional editions across the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
Led the National Newspaper Publishers Association in 1954–55.

legacyDetail.d: The Murphy family has controlled the Afro for more than a century.

name: Carl Ware
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in political science from Clark College, then an MPA from the University of Pittsburgh; later attended Harvard Business School's senior management program (1991).
humbleBeginnings: Built his early career in Atlanta civic life before moving into corporate leadership.
breakthrough: Elected to the Atlanta City Council in 1973 and served as its president (1976–79), then joined Coca-Cola USA in 1979 as VP of special markets, becoming senior VP in 1986 and president of its Africa Group in 1993.
legacy: Executive vice president of the Coca-Cola Company (2001–2003) and senior adviser to the CEO (2003–06); director of Chevron.

breakthroughDetail.d: Ran Coca-Cola's Africa Group from 1993.
One of Coca-Cola's top executives.

legacyDetail.d: Served on the board of Chevron Corporation.

sources.label: AUC Woodruff Library — Carl Ware papers

name: Carla Walker-Miller
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in civil engineering from Tennessee State University on a full scholarship.
humbleBeginnings: Worked for an engineering firm and sold energy equipment before starting her own company.
breakthrough: Founded Walker-Miller Energy Services in 2000, pivoting it into energy-efficiency programs for utilities and becoming one of Detroit's leading Black-owned firms.
legacy: Serves as founder and CEO, completed Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses (2014), and joined The Henry Ford's board of trustees in 2020.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founder and CEO of Walker-Miller Energy Services.
Participated in Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses in 2014.

legacyDetail.d: Wikipedia describes her as an entrepreneur and Detroit booster.

name: Carrie Meek
hbcuStory: Graduated from Florida A&M in 1946, where she was also a track athlete.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Tallahassee's segregated Black community.
breakthrough: Became one of the first three Black Floridians elected to Congress since Reconstruction (1992).
legacy: Represented Miami in Congress 1993–2003; succeeded by her son Kendrick Meek, also a FAMU graduate.

legacyDetail.d: Son Kendrick Meek succeeded her.

name: Cathy Hughes
wealthNote: No reliable current figure; Wikipedia notes she was once listed as the second-richest Black woman in the U.S. after Oprah Winfrey.
hbcuStory: Not a Howard graduate: she came to Howard in 1971 as an administrative assistant/lecturer in the new School of Communications under Tony Brown, then ran sales and later management at the university's WHUR-FM, where she created the 'Quiet Storm' format. Howard renamed its School of Communications for her in 2016.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Omaha in 1947, she became a mother at 17 and took business administration courses at the University of Nebraska Omaha and Creighton without finishing a degree; she started in radio at KOWH in 1969.
breakthrough: As WHUR's general sales manager from 1973 she grew station revenue from $250,000 to $3 million in a year, and in 1975 became the first woman general manager of a D.C. station. In 1980, after 32 bank rejections, she and Dewey Hughes bought WOL-AM and founded Radio One.
legacy: Radio One (now Urban One) went public in 1999, making her the first African American woman to head a publicly traded company; it launched TV One in 2004 and is the largest Black-owned U.S. broadcaster. Control passed to her son Alfred Liggins III as CEO while she remains chair.

humbleBeginnings: Youngest of 15 children of a San Antonio educator-farmer; his brother G. J. Sutton also became a businessman and legislator.

Manhattan Borough President and a member of Harlem's ‘Gang of Four’.

humbleBeginnings: Born in Westfield, Mass., son of a barber; worked as a janitor in a New York real estate office before starting his own agency.

Iconic TV role.

name: Q. V. Williamson

humbleBeginnings: Born in Atlanta and educated at Booker T. Washington High School.
breakthrough: Built Q. V. Williamson & Company, a real estate brokerage, and helped develop the Black middle-class Collier Heights neighborhood; in 1965 became the first Black member of Atlanta's Board of Aldermen since Reconstruction.

humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in Noxubee County, Mississippi; worked as a cowboy and laborer in Texas before becoming a Baptist minister.

legacy: Co-founded and was first president of One-Cent Savings Bank (1904), still operating as Citizens Savings Bank and Trust — one of the oldest Black-owned banks — and launched the National Negro Doll Company.

One-Cent Savings Bank (1904) became Citizens Savings Bank and Trust.
Sold and then manufactured Black dolls (1908–c.1915).

name: Ralph Ellison
